scope: Two to four key references per computational lesson: at least one foundational or standard-tool work and at least one published in 2019 or later. Every entry is checked by scripts/verify_references.py; results are in reference_verification.json.

lessons.technique: Input-to-output transformation contracts, axis semantics, and temporal scaling invariants (demeaning, percent signal change, z-scoring)
lessons.why_it_matters: Every neuroimaging preprocessing and modeling step transforms array shapes, physical units, and statistical conditioning sets. Without an explicit transformation contract, a syntactically valid snippet can demean across space instead of time (passing a naive global-mean check while injecting global-signal artifacts) or alter group-level GLM effect sizes (beta_hat) across coil sensitivity profiles even though single-voxel t-statistics remain invariant.

lessons.technique: Bloch relaxation (T1, T2, T2*), Gradient-Echo BOLD sensitivity, and neurovascular hemodynamic coupling
lessons.why_it_matters: MRI voxel intensities are sequence-weighted echo amplitudes rather than direct measurements of tissue density or spiking activity. Understanding how TR, TE, and flip angle invert tissue contrast, why BOLD contrast peaks near TE = T2* while suffering susceptibility dropout near air-tissue sinuses, and why BOLD reflects perisynaptic LFP input filtered through a sluggish, region-specific hemodynamic response (Logothetis et al., 2001) prevents reverse-inference and vascular-latency confounds in fMRI.

references.takeaway: Synthesizes modern cellular and vascular mechanisms of neurovascular coupling, highlighting how interneurons, non-neural drives, and regional vascular dynamics shape BOLD signals.

lessons.technique: Forensic Python/NumPy code auditing: broadcasting semantics, domain guards, view vs. copy aliasing, mask indexing, and fold-isolated feature selection
lessons.why_it_matters: The most dangerous bugs in scientific Python are silent semantic errors that execute without raising exceptions—such as missing keepdims=True on square matrices, mutating shared-memory NumPy slice views in place, averaging across unmasked background zeros, or screening features before cross-validation (Kriegeskorte et al., 2009; Rosenblatt et al., 2024). Auditing code line-by-line as a mathematical contract prevents fabricated decoding accuracy and corrupted baselines.

lessons.technique: Jupyter kernel state hygiene, PRNG stream isolation (SeedSequence), IEEE-754 floating-point determinism, and cryptographic provenance

Distinguishing bitwise SHA-256 reproducibility, numerical tolerance reproducibility (under IEEE-754 float32 non-associativity and catastrophic cancellation), and scientific replicability is essential for trustworthy neuroimaging workflows (Glatard et al., 2015).

lessons.technique: Voxel-to-world affine geometry, NIfTI qform/sform headers, and BIDS metadata contracts
lessons.why_it_matters: Every neuroimaging operation—from cross-modal EPI-to-T1w registration and susceptibility distortion unwarping in fMRIPrep to 3D keypoint alignment in BrainMorph—depends on mapping discrete 0-indexed voxel arrays into continuous physical millimeter coordinates (RAS+) and reading pulse-sequence timing from BIDS JSON sidecars. Stripping NIfTI affines (resetting to an identity matrix), flipping array axes without post-multiplying the affine by the corresponding reflection-translation matrix, or ignoring sform/qform shear divergence silently swaps cerebral hemispheres or shifts coordinates by tens of millimeters without altering image intensity histograms. Mastering the 4x4 homogeneous affine decomposition and header precedence rules forces explicit verification of handedness (sign of det(M)), voxel volume (|det(M)|), and BIDS metadata completeness before running any downstream model.

lessons.technique: Affine image registration, similarity cost functions, backward pull resampling, and interpolation transfer functions
lessons.why_it_matters: Aligning multi-modal and longitudinal brain scans requires decoupling transformation estimation (via intensity cost functions like Mutual Information or closed-form keypoint least squares) from grid resampling. Forward ('push') coordinate rounding creates unvisited grid holes and collisions, interpolating discrete parcellation masks with linear or spline kernels fabricates invalid anatomical label IDs along ROI boundaries, and applying sequential resamplings across pipeline stages compounds low-pass spatial filtering that biases smoothness-dependent statistical inference. Understanding backward ('pull') sampling, kernel frequency responses, and single-shot composed transformations is essential for building artifact-free registration workflows in FSL FLIRT, ANTs, fMRIPrep, and BrainMorph.

lessons.technique: Nonlinear deformable registration, Jacobian determinant topology auditing, spatial regularization, and stationary velocity field integration
lessons.why_it_matters: Nonlinear registration aligns subject-specific cortical folding and subcortical morphology to a common template using millions of displacement parameters, making the optimization inherently ill-posed without spatial regularization. An unregularized warp can achieve deceptively high intensity similarity or regional Dice overlap while folding tissue over itself (non-positive Jacobian determinant, J(x) <= 0), destroying anatomical topology and invalidating downstream cortical surface projection or morphometry. Computing the deformation gradient tensor F(x) = I + grad u(x), auditing log-Jacobian maps and folding percentages, and integrating stationary velocity fields via scaling-and-squaring (phi = exp(v)) are mandatory to guarantee invertible, diffeomorphic transformations.

lessons.technique: Bias-field (RF intensity non-uniformity) modeling, homomorphic log-filtering, and N4ITK correction
lessons.why_it_matters: Radiofrequency transmit (B1+) standing-wave interference and phased-array receive (B1-) coil sensitivity drop-off modulate true tissue contrast by a smooth multiplicative gain field B(x) that scales both class means and within-tissue variances (proportionally to mu_c^2). Left uncorrected, low-frequency shading causes white matter in dimly illuminated regions to fall below gray matter intensities in bright peripheral regions, breaking global thresholds, Gaussian mixture models, and registration cost functions. Transforming intensities into the log domain (homomorphic filtering) and applying iterative histogram sharpening with B-spline basis constraints (N4ITK) or generative bias randomization (SynthSeg) removes coil shading while enforcing scale separation so anatomical contrast and focal lesions are not erased.

lessons.technique: Brain extraction (skull stripping), boundary distance metrics (HD95, ASSD), and downstream morphometric/registration error cascades
lessons.why_it_matters: Brain extraction defines the spatial domain for downstream bias correction, tissue segmentation, inter-modal coregistration, and cortical surface reconstruction. Because the cerebral cortex is a thin outer ribbon (~2-4 mm) surrounding a large interior volume, whole-brain volumetric Dice is mathematically insensitive to superficial cortical erosion (over-stripping that causes fake cortical atrophy in FreeSurfer/FastSurfer) as well as localized dural, marrow, or orbital retention (under-stripping that pulls pial surfaces outward, biases intensity clustering thresholds, and shifts registration centers of mass). Auditing brain masks therefore requires multi-slice contour overlays alongside surface distance metrics (HD95, ASSD) and compartment-specific cortical ribbon recall.

references.takeaway: Establishes HD-BET, demonstrating that 3D U-Net brain extraction generalizes across multisequence clinical MRI scans and pathological brains.

lessons.technique: Probabilistic tissue segmentation, Gaussian Mixture Models with EM, Markov Random Field priors, and partial-volume estimation
lessons.why_it_matters: Brain tissue segmentation partitions structural MRI into cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), gray matter (GM), and white matter (WM) for morphometry and surface reconstruction, but finite voxel resolution causes boundary voxels to contain mixtures of multiple tissues (partial volume effects, PVE). Because CSF (~30) and WM (~110) average to the intensity of pure GM (~75) on T1w MRI, pointwise classifiers without spatial neighborhood priors (such as FSL FAST's HMRF/Potts model or 3D contextual CNNs like SynthSeg) fabricate a false rim of gray matter around the ventricles, while winner-take-all argmax thresholding systematically erases thin cortical ribbons on thick-slice scans. Distinguishing discrete MAP labels, Bayesian posterior probabilities, and physical partial-volume fractions is essential for unbiased regional volume estimation.

lessons.technique: Volumetric morphometry, VBM Jacobian modulation, and Total Intracranial Volume (TIV) adjustment
lessons.why_it_matters: Structural MRI segmentation masks only become valid biological volume measurements when calibrated by physical voxel volume (|det(M)|), modulated by the nonlinear warp Jacobian determinant in template space (Voxel-Based Morphometry), and adjusted for premorbid head size (Total Intracranial Volume, TIV/eTIV). Without these steps, scanner resolution differences alter raw voxel counts up to 9-fold, nonlinear registration erases true regional atrophy in unmodulated template maps, and sampling imbalances in head size can reverse the sign of group atrophy comparisons (Simpson's Paradox). Researchers must choose between native-space ROI integration vs. Jacobian-modulated VBM, linear control-slope residualization vs. proportional/allometric TIV scaling, and cross-sectional vs. longitudinal within-subject designs.

lessons.technique: Cortical surface triangular meshes, Euler-Poincare topology verification, cortical thickness, and geodesic smoothing
lessons.why_it_matters: The human cerebral cortex is a tightly folded 2D sheet where opposing banks of a sulcus are separated by only 2-3 mm across CSF in 3D Euclidean space but 20-30 mm along the cortical ribbon. Surface-based pipelines (FreeSurfer, FastSurfer, HCP/fMRIPrep CIFTI) require each hemisphere's white-matter surface to be topologically homeomorphic to a 2-sphere (genus g = 0, Euler characteristic chi = 2) before spherical inflation, inter-subject registration, vertex-wise thickness estimation, and geodesic smoothing can be performed. Because a single-voxel bridge across a sulcus changes volumetric Dice by <0.1% while turning the surface into a genus-1 torus (chi = 0), researchers must explicitly audit and repair mesh topology rather than relying on volumetric segmentation metrics.

lessons.technique: fMRI slice-timing acquisition schedules and Fourier phase-shift vs. linear temporal interpolation
lessons.why_it_matters: Standard 2D echo-planar imaging (EPI) acquires slices sequentially or in interleaved/multiband groups across the Repetition Time (TR), so physically adjacent slices in an interleaved scan can be sampled half a TR (e.g., 1.0 s) apart. In event-related and short-block task fMRI, uncorrected slice-timing offsets shift the hemodynamic response relative to the GLM design matrix, attenuating beta estimates in late-acquired slices and introducing odd/even sawtooth artifacts across axial slices. Because NIfTI headers frequently omit slice timing, pipelines such as fMRIPrep require explicit BIDS SliceTiming metadata and skip correction rather than guessing a schedule that could corrupt phase alignment.

lessons.technique: fMRI rigid-body head-motion realignment, Framewise Displacement (FD), DVARS, Friston-24 expansion, and frame censoring (scrubbing)
lessons.why_it_matters: Six-degree-of-freedom rigid-body realignment corrects spatial coordinates across volumes but cannot undo physical NMR signal disruptions caused by out-of-plane spin-history (T1 steady-state excitation) perturbations, motion-by-susceptibility field changes, and intra-volume motion. In resting-state functional connectivity MRI, these residual shared intensity transients systematically inflate short-range correlations and weaken long-range network connections even after 6-parameter regression. Researchers must quantify Framewise Displacement (FD) and DVARS, apply Volterra expansion (Friston-24) and targeted spike regression/censoring without introducing temporal filtering artifacts, and enforce group-matched participant retention policies to prevent selection bias.

lessons.technique: EPI susceptibility distortion correction (fieldmap and reversed phase-encode TOPUP unwarping) vs. intra-voxel T2* signal dropout
lessons.why_it_matters: Single-shot echo-planar imaging (EPI) used in fMRI and dMRI has a very low bandwidth along the phase-encoding axis (~15-35 Hz/voxel), causing magnetic susceptibility gradients near the sinuses and ear canals to stretch or compress brain anatomy by 4-15 mm while simultaneously causing irreversible through-slice T2* dephasing dropout in orbitofrontal and inferior temporal cortices. Accurate susceptibility distortion correction (FSL TOPUP, FUGUE, SDCflows) requires verified BIDS PhaseEncodingDirection polarity and TotalReadoutTime metadata to restore geometric alignment to structural T1w anatomy, and researchers must mask out unrecoverable T2* dropout voids rather than assuming geometric unwarping restores lost BOLD signal.

references.authors: Jezzard P, Balaban RS
references.title: Correction for geometric distortion in echo planar images from B0 field variations
references.takeaway: Derives the physics of B0 susceptibility-induced phase-encoding voxel shifts in echo-planar imaging and demonstrates fieldmap-based geometric unwarping.

references.authors: Andersson JL, Skare S, Ashburner J
references.title: How to correct susceptibility distortions in spin-echo echo-planar images: application to diffusion tensor imaging
references.takeaway: Formulates the reversed phase-encoding model (implemented in FSL TOPUP) that estimates the off-resonance displacement field and Jacobian modulation from opposing-polarity EPI acquisitions.

references.authors: Ojemann JG, Akbudak E, Snyder AZ, McKinstry RC, Raichle ME, Conturo TE
references.title: Anatomic Localization and Quantitative Analysis of Gradient Refocused Echo-Planar fMRI Susceptibility Artifacts
references.takeaway: Characterizes both geometric distortion and irreversible through-slice T2* dephasing signal loss in gradient-echo EPI near the sinuses and petrous bone.

references.authors: Schilling KG, Blaber J, Hansen C, Cai L, Rogers B, Anderson AW, Smith S, Kanakaraj P, Rex T, Resnick SM, Shafer AT, Cutting LE, Woodward N, Zald D, Landman BA
references.title: Distortion correction of diffusion weighted MRI without reverse phase-encoding scans or field-maps
references.takeaway: Introduces deep-learning synthetic undistorted b0 generation (Synb0-DisCo) from structural T1w MRI to enable TOPUP susceptibility distortion correction when reversed phase-encode scans are unavailable.

lessons.technique: Volumetric, mask-normalized, and surface-geodesic spatial smoothing
lessons.why_it_matters: Spatial smoothing trades spatial resolution for thermal SNR and inter-subject overlap in mass-univariate GLM analyses (`FSL SUSAN`, `SPM`, `AFNI 3dBlurToFWHM`), while pipelines like `fMRIPrep` (`PP01`) intentionally omit it to keep derivatives analysis-agnostic. Applying an isotropic 3D volumetric Gaussian kernel across the folded $2\text{--}3\;\text{mm}$ cortical ribbon mixes signal across sulcal CSF gaps and subcortical nuclei boundaries (Coalson et al., 2018; Sacchet & Knutson, 2013) and destroys fine-scale MVPA/laminar patterns. Researchers must choose the smoothing domain (volumetric vs. mask-normalized vs. cortical-surface geodesic via `wb_command -cifti-smoothing`), convert physical $\text{FWHM}_{\text{mm}}$ per axis on anisotropic grids, and match kernel scale to expected activation extent (Worsley et al., 1996; Blazejewska et al., 2019).

references.authors: Worsley KJ, Marrett S, Neelin P, Evans AC
references.title: Searching scale space for activation in PET images
references.takeaway: Establishes the matched-filter scale-space framework and Random Field Theory resel geometry showing that detection sensitivity peaks when filter width matches true activation scale.

references.authors: Mikl M, Mareček R, Hluštík P, Pavlicová M, Drastich A, Chlebus P
references.title: Effects of spatial smoothing on fMRI group inferences
references.takeaway: Quantifies how varying spatial smoothing kernel widths systematically shifts cluster extent, peak coordinates, and false-negative rates in group-level fMRI inference.

references.authors: Coalson TS, Van Essen DC, Glasser MF
references.title: The impact of traditional neuroimaging methods on the spatial localization of cortical areas
references.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
references.takeaway: Demonstrates that traditional 3D volumetric smoothing and volumetric registration severely degrade cortical areal localization compared with surface-based geodesic processing.

references.authors: Blazejewska AI, Fischl B, Wald LL, Polimeni JR
references.title: Intracortical smoothing of small-voxel fMRI data can provide increased detection power without spatial resolution losses compared to conventional large-voxel fMRI data
references.takeaway: Shows that anatomically informed intracortical and laminar-constrained smoothing of small-voxel fMRI data increases detection sensitivity without blurring across cortical banks or CSF.

lessons.technique: Temporal filtering, physiological aliasing, DCT drift projection, and effective degrees of freedom
lessons.why_it_matters: Every task and resting-state fMRI pipeline (`SPM`, `FSL FEAT`, `AFNI 3dTproject`, `fMRIPrep` DCT confounds) must remove slow scanner drift ($<0.01\;\text{Hz}$) while accounting for physiological noise aliasing and hemodynamic passband limits (`PB01`). Misconfiguring temporal filters—such as passing uncalibrated sampling rates `fs`, band-pass filtering across uncensored motion spikes, or ignoring filter-induced autocorrelation—either attenuates true neural variance, smears transient artifacts across $\pm 30\;\text{s}$ of clean frames (Carp, 2013; Power et al., 2014), or inflates false-positive connectivity by collapsing effective degrees of freedom $\nu_{\text{eff}}$ (Davey et al., 2013). Researchers must coordinate filter cutoffs with task design frequencies, TR-dependent Nyquist limits, and simultaneous confound regression (Hallquist et al., 2013; Lindquist et al., 2019).

references.authors: Friston K, Josephs O, Zarahn E, Holmes A, Rouquette S, Poline J
references.title: To Smooth or Not to Smooth?
references.takeaway: Formalizes the bias-efficiency trade-off of temporal filtering and smoothing in fMRI time-series general linear models.

references.authors: Davey CE, Grayden DB, Egan GF, Johnston LA
references.title: Filtering induces correlation in fMRI resting state data
references.takeaway: Proves how band-pass filtering induces temporal autocorrelation that reduces effective degrees of freedom and inflates null functional connectivity variance.

references.authors: Hallquist MN, Hwang K, Luna B
references.title: The nuisance of nuisance regression: Spectral misspecification in a common approach to resting-state fMRI preprocessing reintroduces noise and obscures functional connectivity
references.takeaway: Demonstrates that sequential mismatch between temporal band-pass filtering and nuisance regression reintroduces spectral noise artifacts into resting-state connectivity.

references.authors: Lindquist MA, Geuter S, Wager TD, Caffo BS
references.title: Modular preprocessing pipelines can reintroduce artifacts into fMRI data
references.takeaway: Proves via orthogonal projection geometry that modular preprocessing steps (filtering, censoring, and confound regression) do not commute and must be combined or co-filtered.

lessons.technique: Nuisance regression, anatomical CompCor (aCompCor), Global Signal Regression (GSR), ICA denoising, and orthogonal projection
lessons.why_it_matters: Nuisance denoising is required in functional connectivity and task fMRI because sub-millimeter head motion and physiological pulsations induce structured covariance across the brain (`PP02`), yet denoising strategy choice remains a primary driver of analytic variability across studies (Ciric et al., 2017; Parkes et al., 2018; `PD01`). Sequential modular pipelines that regress unfiltered confounds after temporal filtering reintroduce previously removed stopband drift because non-commuting subspace projections are not orthogonal (Lindquist et al., 2019; Hallquist et al., 2013). Researchers must construct simultaneous or identically filtered design matrices (e.g., pairing `fMRIPrep` `a_comp_cor_XX` components with `cosine_XX` drift bases) and weigh the physiological specificity of eroded WM/CSF `aCompCor` (Behzadi et al., 2007) and `ICA-AROMA` (Pruim et al., 2015) against the zero-sum covariance shift of Global Signal Regression (Murphy et al., 2009; Murphy & Fox, 2017) and degrees-of-freedom exhaustion.

references.authors: Behzadi Y, Restom K, Liau J, Liu TT
references.title: A component based noise correction method (CompCor) for BOLD and perfusion based fMRI
references.takeaway: Introduces anatomical and temporal CompCor, extracting principal components from eroded white-matter and CSF masks to remove physiological and motion noise without global signal regression.

references.authors: Pruim RH, Mennes M, van Rooij D, Llera A, Buitelaar JK, Beckmann CF
references.title: ICA-AROMA: A robust ICA-based strategy for removing motion artifacts from fMRI data
references.takeaway: Establishes ICA-AROMA, a four-feature spatial/temporal/spectral classifier that identifies motion-related independent components for non-aggressive partial regression.

references.authors: Ciric R, Wolf DH, Power JD, Roalf DR, Baum GL, Ruparel K
references.title: Benchmarking of participant-level confound regression strategies for the control of motion artifact in studies of functional connectivity
references.takeaway: Benchmarks 14 participant-level confound regression pipelines across QC-FC distance dependence, temporal degrees of freedom loss, and network modularity.

references.authors: Wang H, Meisler SL, Sharmarke H, Clarke N, Gensollen N, Markiewicz CJ
references.title: Continuous evaluation of denoising strategies in resting-state fMRI connectivity using fMRIPrep and Nilearn
references.takeaway: Provides a modern continuous benchmark of resting-state fMRI denoising workflows across BIDS derivatives, quantifying trade-offs between motion removal and signal preservation.

lessons.technique: Framewise Displacement (FD), DVARS, carpet-plot quality control, motion censoring (scrubbing), and spike regression
lessons.why_it_matters: Transient head movements during EPI readout disrupt spin history and create distance-dependent functional connectivity biases (inflating short-range correlations and weakening long-range connections) that survive linear motion regression (`PP02`, Power et al., 2012, 2014). Quality-control pipelines (`fMRIPrep` `PP01`, `MRIQC` Esteban et al., 2017) pair Framewise Displacement (FD) and DVARS traces with voxelwise carpet plots (Power, 2017) and output one-hot `motion_outlier_XX` spike regressors (Lemieux et al., 2007; Afyouni & Nichols, 2018) to censor corrupted frames without breaking temporal indexing. Researchers must set principled per-frame censoring and minimum-duration exclusion rules while accounting for the demographic selection bias introduced when high-motion youth, older adults, or clinical participants are disproportionately excluded (Satterthwaite et al., 2012; Nebel et al., 2022).

references.authors: Power JD, Mitra A, Laumann TO, Snyder AZ, Schlaggar BL, Petersen SE
references.title: Methods to detect, characterize, and remove motion artifact in resting state fMRI
references.takeaway: Establishes comprehensive FD/DVARS motion scrubbing protocols, spectral interpolation prior to filtering, and minimum clean-data duration benchmarks for resting-state fMRI.

references.authors: Esteban O, Birman D, Schaer M, Koyejo OO, Poldrack RA, Gorgolewski KJ
references.title: MRIQC: Advancing the automatic prediction of image quality in MRI from unseen sites
references.takeaway: Introduces MRIQC for automated extraction of image quality metrics (including FD, DVARS, and SNR) and visual quality-control reporting across BIDS datasets.

references.authors: Afyouni S, Nichols TE
references.title: Insight and inference for DVARS
references.takeaway: Derives the null distribution and standardized scaling of DVARS, enabling formal statistical hypothesis testing for framewise intensity spikes.

references.authors: Nebel MB, Lidstone DE, Wang L, Benkeser D, Mostofsky SH, Risk BB
references.title: Accounting for motion in resting-state fMRI: What part of the spectrum are we characterizing in autism spectrum disorder?
references.takeaway: Quantifies how strict motion censoring and participant exclusion thresholds disproportionately remove clinically severe and younger participants, biasing group-level inference.

lessons.technique: Diffusion MRI q-space encoding, B-table (.bval/.bvec) synchronization, and polar-decomposition gradient reorientation
lessons.why_it_matters: In diffusion MRI (`FSL eddy`, `QSIPrep` `PP08`, `MRtrix3`, `DIPY`), the 4th array dimension indexes 3D q-space sensitization vectors $(b_n, \mathbf{g}_n)$ rather than uniform temporal samples, coupling voxel geometry directly to directional metadata. Failing to rotate $\mathbf{g}_n$ by the rigid-body realignment matrix $R_n$ after head motion biases principal eigenvectors and fractional anisotropy (Leemans & Jones, 2009), while axis sign flips ($g_x \to -g_x$) leave scalar FA and MD maps completely unchanged yet mirror fiber orientations across the sagittal plane and wreck tractography (`PP06`, Jeurissen et al., 2014; Schilling et al., 2019). Researchers must preserve the volume-to-gradient bijection, mask $b_0$ shells before vector normalization, and extract pure proper rotations $R \in \text{SO}(3)$ via polar decomposition (Alexander et al., 2001) rather than applying non-orthogonal shear affines directly to $\mathbf{g}_n$.

references.authors: Basser P, Mattiello J, LeBihan D
references.title: MR diffusion tensor spectroscopy and imaging
references.takeaway: Introduces Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI), formulating the quadratic Stejskal-Tanner log-signal model connecting directional gradient encodings to the symmetric diffusion tensor.

references.authors: Leemans A, Jones DK
references.title: The B-matrix must be rotated when correcting for subject motion in DTI data
references.takeaway: Demonstrates that failing to rotate the B-matrix alongside motion-realigned diffusion volumes systematically biases tensor eigenvalues, principal eigenvectors, and tractography.

references.authors: Andersson JL, Sotiropoulos SN
references.title: An integrated approach to correction for off-resonance effects and subject movement in diffusion MR imaging
references.takeaway: Establishes FSL eddy for joint off-resonance and movement correction in diffusion MRI, outputting motion-rotated gradient tables (.eddy_rotated_bvecs).

references.authors: Schilling KG, Yeh F, Nath V, Hansen C, Williams O, Resnick S
references.title: A fiber coherence index for quality control of B-table orientation in diffusion MRI scans
references.takeaway: Introduces an automated fiber coherence quality-control index that detects axis flips and coordinate-frame swaps in diffusion B-tables that scalar FA maps cannot reveal.

lessons.technique: Diffusion MRI preprocessing: MP-PCA thermal denoising, Gibbs unringing, susceptibility/eddy distortion correction, and single-step composed interpolation
lessons.why_it_matters: Diffusion MRI encodes microstructural and tract-orientation information in directional signal attenuations across dozens of q-space volumes, making it vulnerable to low-SNR thermal noise, Rician noise-floor bias at high b-values, Fourier truncation ringing at CSF-white matter boundaries, and gradient-dependent eddy-current warps. Standard pipelines such as QSIPrep (Cieslak et al., 2021) and MRtrix3 enforce a non-commutative ordering because spatial interpolation correlates voxelwise noise (violating the i.i.d. assumption of Marchenko-Pastur PCA; Veraart et al., 2016) and alters the native Fourier grid required by subvoxel Gibbs unringing (Kellner et al., 2016). Composing susceptibility, eddy-current, and motion transforms into a single final resampling step with B-table rotation preserves anatomical edge sharpness and prevents directional bias in downstream tensor and tractography models.

references.authors: Veraart J, Novikov DS, Christiaens D, Ades-Aron B, Sijbers J, Fieremans E
references.title: Denoising of diffusion MRI using random matrix theory
references.takeaway: Introduces Marchenko-Pastur PCA (MP-PCA) for local thermal noise estimation and suppression, demonstrating why denoising must precede any spatial interpolation that correlates noise across voxels.

references.authors: Kellner E, Dhital B, Kiselev VG, Reisert M
references.title: Gibbs-ringing artifact removal based on local subvoxel-shifts
references.takeaway: Establishes local subvoxel-shift re-interpolation to sample sinc zero-crossings and remove k-space truncation ringing prior to nonlinear distortion warping.

references.authors: Andersson JLR, Sotiropoulos SN
references.title: An integrated approach to correction for off-resonance effects and subject movement in diffusion MR imaging
references.takeaway: Defines the standard Gaussian-process EDDY framework that jointly models susceptibility off-resonance fields, gradient-dependent eddy currents, and head motion.

references.authors: Tax CMW, Bastiani M, Veraart J, Garyfallidis E, Okan Irfanoglu M
references.title: What’s new and what’s next in diffusion MRI preprocessing
references.takeaway: Synthesizes modern dMRI preprocessing stages, their non-commutative ordering dependencies, and remaining challenges across denoising, unringing, and distortion correction.

lessons.technique: Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI): 6-parameter B-matrix design, OLS vs. heteroscedastic WLS estimation, spectral invariants (MD, AD, RD, FA), and Westin shape indices
lessons.why_it_matters: Diffusion Tensor Imaging (Basser et al., 1994) is the most widely deployed microstructural MRI model in clinical and cognitive neuroscience, summarizing directional water diffusivity via scalar invariants such as Fractional Anisotropy (FA) and Mean Diffusivity (MD). Without understanding heteroscedastic log-domain noise (Salvador et al., 2005; Veraart et al., 2013), unweighted OLS fits over-weight noisy high-attenuation directions, and without checking physical MD units, scale-invariant FA masks 1000x b-value unit errors. Crucially, because 60%–90% of white-matter voxels contain crossing fibers (Jeurissen et al., 2013), a single tensor collapses into an oblate ellipsoid with reduced FA, forcing researchers to use Westin shape indices or multi-fiber models rather than misinterpreting lower FA as demyelination (Jones et al., 2013; Figley et al., 2022).

references.authors: Basser PJ, Mattiello J, LeBihan D
references.title: MR diffusion tensor spectroscopy and imaging
references.takeaway: Formulates the 3x3 symmetric diffusion tensor model and linear B-matrix estimation from directional Stejskal-Tanner measurements.

references.authors: Pierpaoli C, Basser PJ
references.title: Toward a quantitative assessment of diffusion anisotropy
references.takeaway: Defines Fractional Anisotropy (FA) and characterizes how thermal noise induces eigenvalue sorting bias in anisotropic and isotropic tissues.

references.authors: Jones DK, Knösche TR, Turner R
references.title: White matter integrity, fiber count, and other fallacies: The do's and don'ts of diffusion MRI
references.takeaway: Explains why scalar FA is non-specific to myelination or axonal integrity because crossing fibers, partial volume, and acquisition noise alter eigenvalue dispersion.

references.authors: Figley CR, Uddin MN, Wong K, Kornelsen J, Puig J, Figley TD
references.title: Potential Pitfalls of Using Fractional Anisotropy, Axial Diffusivity, and Radial Diffusivity as Biomarkers of Cerebral White Matter Microstructure
references.takeaway: Demonstrates how crossing fibers and partial-volume effects confound voxelwise FA, AD, and RD interpretations in clinical and neuroimaging studies.

lessons.technique: Crossing-fiber spherical deconvolution (CSD / fODF) and deterministic/probabilistic streamline tractography
lessons.why_it_matters: Because most white-matter voxels contain crossing or fanning axon bundles, single-tensor tractography terminates prematurely or follows false diagonal averages, motivating Fiber Orientation Distribution Function (fODF) estimation via Constrained Spherical Deconvolution (Tournier et al., 2007; Jeurissen et al., 2014). However, as the ISMRM 2015 Tractography Challenge demonstrated (Maier-Hein et al., 2017, PP06), even exact local fiber orientations cannot prevent streamlines from taking false exit branches after merging into shared anatomical bottlenecks such as the internal capsule or temporal stem. Understanding ODE integration step-size errors, angular stopping criteria, anatomical priors (ACT), and tractogram filtering (SIFT2) is essential before interpreting streamline counts as structural connectivity.

references.authors: Tournier J-D, Calamante F, Connelly A
references.title: Robust determination of the fibre orientation distribution in diffusion MRI: Non-negativity constrained super-resolved spherical deconvolution
references.takeaway: Establishes Constrained Spherical Deconvolution (CSD) to resolve multiple intra-voxel fiber orientations by deconvolving the single-fiber response kernel under non-negativity constraints.

references.authors: Behrens TEJ, Berg HJ, Jbabdi S, Rushworth MFS, Woolrich MW
references.title: Probabilistic diffusion tractography with multiple fibre orientations: What can we gain?
references.takeaway: Demonstrates why modeling multiple fiber orientations per voxel is required to recover non-dominant pathways in probabilistic tractography (FSL bedpostx/probtrackx).

references.authors: Maier-Hein KH, Neher PF, Houde J-C, Côté M-A, Garyfallidis E, et al.
references.title: The challenge of mapping the human connectome based on diffusion tractography
references.takeaway: Shows across 96 tractography submissions that algorithms recover up to 90% of true bundles but generate on average more than 4x as many invalid bundles due to shared anatomical bottlenecks.

references.authors: Jeurissen B, Descoteaux M, Mori S, Leemans A
references.title: Diffusion MRI fiber tractography of the brain
references.takeaway: Reviews local orientation modeling, deterministic and probabilistic ODE integration, anatomical constraints, and false-positive/false-negative tradeoffs in brain tractography.

lessons.technique: Atlas parcellation, voxel-coverage auditing, confound-regressed functional/structural connectome estimation (Pearson vs. Ledoit-Wolf partial correlation), and out-of-fold Connectome-Based Predictive Modeling (CPM)
lessons.why_it_matters: Parcellation compresses tens of thousands of noisy voxel series into P regional nodes and P(P-1)/2 connectome edges for network neuroscience and clinical prediction (Glasser et al., 2016; Schaefer et al., 2018; Shen et al., 2017). Without auditing valid voxel coverage fractions and nearest-neighbor label alignment, susceptibility dropout in orbitofrontal and temporal cortex silently injects thermal noise or mixes adjacent regions inside a syntactically valid P x P matrix. Furthermore, because shared motion inflates marginal Pearson correlations (Power et al., 2012; Ciric et al., 2017) and edge dimensions vastly exceed cohort sizes, researchers must choose between full and shrinkage-regularized partial correlation (Smith et al., 2011; Pervaiz et al., 2020) and confine feature screening strictly within cross-validation folds.

references.authors: Glasser MF, Coalson TS, Robinson EC, Hacker CD, Harwell J, et al.
references.title: A multi-modal parcellation of human cerebral cortex
references.takeaway: Defines the 360-area HCP-MMP1.0 cortical parcellation by integrating myelin, thickness, task fMRI, and resting-state functional connectivity gradients.

references.authors: Schaefer A, Kong R, Gordon EM, Laumann TO, Zuo X-N, Holmes AJ, Eickhoff SB, Yeo BTT
references.title: Local-Global Parcellation of the Human Cerebral Cortex from Intrinsic Functional Connectivity MRI
references.takeaway: Introduces the multiscale (100–1000 parcel) local-global cortical parcellation widely used in functional and structural connectomics.

references.authors: Smith SM, Miller KL, Salimi-Khorshidi G, Webster M, Beckmann CF, Nichols TE, Ramsey JD, Woolrich MW
references.title: Network modelling methods for FMRI
references.takeaway: Demonstrates on simulated fMRI networks that regularized partial correlation (inverse covariance) separates direct edges from indirect transitive pathways far better than full Pearson correlation.

references.authors: Pervaiz U, Vidaurre D, Woolrich MW, Smith SM
references.title: Optimising network modelling methods for fMRI
references.takeaway: Benchmarks parcellation and covariance/precision estimation strategies (including Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage and tangent-space parameterization) for individual connectome fingerprinting and prediction.

lessons.technique: Workflow DAG scheduling, parameter-aware Merkle-DAG provenance hashing, and visual/quantitative quality-control reporting
lessons.why_it_matters: Modern neuroimaging pipelines such as fMRIPrep (Esteban et al., 2019, PP01) and QSIPrep (Cieslak et al., 2021, PP08) dynamically assemble dozens of processing nodes from BIDS metadata (Gorgolewski et al., 2016) using workflow engines like Nipype (Gorgolewski et al., 2011). Without parameter- and version-aware provenance hashing, changing an upstream hyperparameter silently reuses stale cached derivatives, contributing to unlogged analytic variability across studies (Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020). At the same time, cryptographic hashes and zero exit codes certify only computational reproducibility—not anatomical accuracy—forcing researchers to pair machine-readable provenance with targeted visual and regional QC reports for skull-stripping, boundary-based registration, and motion artifacts (Provins et al., 2023).

references.authors: Gorgolewski K, Burns CD, Madison C, Clark D, Halchenko YO, Waskom ML, Ghosh SS
references.title: Nipype: A Flexible, Lightweight and Extensible Neuroimaging Data Processing Framework in Python
references.takeaway: Introduces the Nipype directed acyclic graph (DAG) execution and parameter-hashed caching architecture underlying fMRIPrep and QSIPrep.

references.authors: Gorgolewski KJ, Auer T, Calhoun VD, Craddock RC, Das S, et al.
references.title: The brain imaging data structure, a format for organizing and describing outputs of neuroimaging experiments
references.takeaway: Defines the BIDS file and JSON sidecar metadata standard that enables automated, metadata-driven workflow construction and derivative provenance.

references.authors: Esteban O, Markiewicz CJ, Blair RW, Moodie CA, Isik AI, et al.
references.title: fMRIPrep: a robust preprocessing pipeline for functional MRI
references.takeaway: Establishes the 'glass-box' preprocessing paradigm combining metadata-driven Nipype DAGs, dynamic citation boilerplate, and self-contained visual HTML QC reports.

references.authors: Provins C, MacNicol E, Seeley SH, Hagmann P, Esteban O
references.title: Quality control in functional MRI studies with MRIQC and fMRIPrep
references.takeaway: Provides a systematic protocol for auditing fMRIPrep and MRIQC visual reports to catch skull-stripping, susceptibility distortion, registration, and motion failures that pass software execution.

lessons.technique: Causal estimands, potential outcomes, DAG identification, and inverse-probability / standardization adjustment
lessons.why_it_matters: Every neuroimaging analysis—from multi-team task-fMRI pipelines (NARPS) to biobank brain-wide association studies (UK Biobank, ABCD)—implicitly targets a specific causal or descriptive estimand before any regression or machine-learning estimator is chosen. Without explicitly specifying the unit-level potential outcomes, target population, and confounder set on a causal DAG, researchers conflate analytical flexibility that changes the scientific question (e.g., conditioning on colliders or altering parametric modulators) with mere estimator variance, and risk severe bias when covariate overlap (positivity) fails across sites or clinical groups.

references.authors: Rubin DB
references.title: Estimating causal effects of treatments in randomized and nonrandomized studies.
references.takeaway: Formalizes causal effects as comparisons of potential outcomes Y(1) and Y(0) on a common set of units, establishing why observational comparisons require explicit assignment-mechanism assumptions.

references.authors: ROSENBAUM PR, RUBIN DB
references.title: The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects
references.takeaway: Introduces the propensity score e(X)=P(A=1|X) and proves that conditioning or weighting on e(X) suffices to remove confounding from observed covariates X under strong ignorability and positivity.

references.authors: Hernán MA, Robins JM
references.title: Estimating causal effects from epidemiological data
references.venue: Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health
references.takeaway: Clearly links potential-outcome estimands, exchangeability, positivity, and consistency to inverse-probability weighting and standardization in observational studies.

references.authors: Lundberg I, Johnson R, Stewart BM
references.title: What Is Your Estimand? Defining the Target Quantity Connects Statistical Evidence to Theory
references.takeaway: Shows why researchers must state the unit-specific quantity, target population, and counterfactual comparison before choosing an estimator or regression specification.

lessons.technique: Hierarchical sampling units, pseudoreplication, missingness mechanisms (MCAR/MAR/MNAR), collider selection bias, and inverse-probability of selection weighting (IPSW)
lessons.why_it_matters: Large-scale neuroimaging cohorts (ABCD, HCP, UK Biobank) combine multi-run, multi-visit, and family-clustered observations with stringent quality-control exclusions (especially head-motion scrubbing) that systematically remove younger participants and individuals with higher clinical symptom severity. Treating repeated scans or twin pairs as independent rows inflates effective sample size by the Kish design effect and causes high false-positive rates (pseudoreplication), while complete-case analysis after motion-related exclusions conditions on a selection collider or MAR/MNAR mechanism that biases brain-behavior estimates unless hierarchical models and inverse-probability retention weights are used.

references.authors: RUBIN DB
references.title: Inference and missing data
references.takeaway: Defines the MCAR, MAR, and MNAR missing-data taxonomy and gives the exact conditions under which missingness mechanisms can be ignored for likelihood or frequentist inference.

references.authors: Hernán MA, Hernández-Díaz S, Robins JM
references.title: A Structural Approach to Selection Bias
references.takeaway: Unifies selection bias across study designs as conditioning on a common effect (collider) of exposure and outcome on a causal DAG, such as analyzing only retained low-motion scans.

references.authors: Lazic SE
references.title: The problem of pseudoreplication in neuroscientific studies: is it affecting your analysis?
references.takeaway: Demonstrates how treating repeated measurements, runs, or related observations as independent sample size N inflates degrees of freedom and Type I error across neuroscience.

references.authors: Nebel MB, Lidstone DE, Wang L, Benkeser D, Mostofsky SH, Risk BB
references.title: Accounting for motion in resting-state fMRI: What part of the spectrum are we characterizing in autism spectrum disorder?
references.takeaway: Treats head-motion quality-control exclusion in developmental and clinical fMRI as an informative missing-data problem and applies inverse-probability / doubly robust weighting to reduce selection bias.

lessons.technique: Classical test theory, intraclass correlation coefficients ICC(2,1) vs ICC(3,1), Spearman-Brown multi-session aggregation, and Spearman attenuation correction
lessons.why_it_matters: A neuroimaging measure that yields a large group-level activation t-statistic can simultaneously fail as an individual-differences biomarker if between-subject variance is small relative to within-subject measurement error—the reliability paradox demonstrated across common task-fMRI paradigms (mean ICC ≈ 0.397; Elliott et al., 2020) and resting-state edges (mean ICC ≈ 0.29; Noble et al., 2019). Choosing between consistency ICC(3,1) and absolute-agreement ICC(2,1) determines whether systematic scanner or longitudinal drift is penalized, while Spearman's attenuation formula shows how reliability ceilings directly cap observable brain-behavior correlations and inflate required sample sizes.

references.authors: Shrout PE, Fleiss JL
references.title: Intraclass correlations: Uses in assessing rater reliability.
references.takeaway: Establishes the classic ANOVA-based intraclass correlation taxonomy, distinguishing random-session agreement ICC(2,1) from fixed-session consistency ICC(3,1) and single- vs k-measurement forms.

references.authors: McGraw KO, Wong SP
references.title: Forming inferences about some intraclass correlation coefficients.
references.takeaway: Formalizes inference and confidence intervals for consistency vs absolute-agreement ICC definitions under two-way random and mixed models.

references.authors: Hedge C, Powell G, Sumner P
references.title: The reliability paradox: Why robust cognitive tasks do not produce reliable individual differences
references.takeaway: Explains the reliability paradox: experimental tasks selected to minimize between-subject variance tau^2 yield strong group-level t-statistics but poor individual-differences reliability.

references.authors: Noble S, Scheinost D, Constable RT
references.title: A decade of test-retest reliability of functional connectivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
references.takeaway: Synthesizes a decade of fMRI functional connectivity test-retest studies (mean edge ICC ~ 0.29), showing how scan duration and aggregation drive reliability for biomarker applications.

lessons.technique: Statistical power, Accuracy in Parameter Estimation (AIPE), Type M/S error design analysis, and group-sequential alpha-spending boundaries
lessons.why_it_matters: Because reproducible univariate brain-wide association effects are typically small (|r| ≈ 0.06–0.16 even in the top 1%; Marek et al., 2022), traditional neuroimaging studies with n = 20–50 have low power and suffer severe Type M exaggeration (winner's curse) and Type S sign errors whenever selection is conditioned on p < 0.05. Prospective design analysis (Gelman & Carlin, 2014), confidence-interval width planning (AIPE), and pre-specified group-sequential alpha-spending boundaries (Pocock, 1977; O'Brien & Fleming, 1979; Lakens, 2022) allow researchers to size cohorts for precision and conduct interim analyses without inflating Type I error.

references.authors: Button KS, Ioannidis JPA, Mokrysz C, Nosek BA, Flint J, Robinson ESJ, Munafò MR
references.title: Power failure: why small sample size undermines the reliability of neuroscience
references.takeaway: Quantifies low statistical power across neuroscience and shows how small samples reduce positive predictive value and inflate significant effect estimates via the winner's curse.

references.authors: Gelman A, Carlin J
references.title: Beyond Power Calculations
references.takeaway: Defines Type M (exaggeration ratio) and Type S (sign error) metrics via design analysis against realistic external effect-size priors rather than post-hoc observed effects.

references.authors: O'Brien PC, Fleming TR
references.title: A Multiple Testing Procedure for Clinical Trials
references.takeaway: Introduces conservative early-look group-sequential stopping boundaries that preserve overall family-wise Type I error alpha while maintaining near-fixed-sample power at the final analysis.

references.authors: Lakens D
references.title: Sample Size Justification
references.takeaway: Provides a modern framework for justifying sample size via power for a smallest effect size of interest, accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE), and sequential designs.

lessons.technique: Neurovascular coupling, linear time-invariant (LTI) hemodynamic convolution, micro-time grid resolution, and frequency-domain design passband analysis
lessons.why_it_matters: First-level task-fMRI general linear models in SPM, FSL, AFNI, and Nilearn rely on modeling the sluggish BOLD signal (peaking ~5–6 s post-stimulus) as the linear time-invariant convolution of sub-TR neural event timings with a canonical hemodynamic response function before downsampling to the scanner TR grid. Understanding LTI convolution, low-pass spectral filtering, micro-time slice-timing alignment, and short-ISI vascular nonlinearities prevents catastrophic regressor misalignment (such as unshifted dummy-scan trimming) and explains why block designs maximize detection SNR while rapid event-related designs require careful spacing.

references.authors: Boynton GM, Engel SA, Glover GH, Heeger DJ
references.title: Linear Systems Analysis of Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging in Human V1
references.takeaway: Establishes empirically in human V1 that BOLD fMRI responses behave approximately as a linear time-invariant convolution of neural stimulus timing over multi-second intervals, with sub-additivity at brief durations.

references.authors: Glover GH
references.title: Deconvolution of Impulse Response in Event-Related BOLD fMRI1
references.takeaway: Characterizes the double-gamma hemodynamic impulse response and shows that linear deconvolution holds when stimuli are separated by >=4 s but breaks down under rapid overlap.

references.authors: Logothetis NK, Pauls J, Augath M, Trinath T, Oeltermann A
references.title: Neurophysiological investigation of the basis of the fMRI signal
references.takeaway: Demonstrates with simultaneous intracortical physiology and fMRI that the BOLD impulse response reflects local field potentials (synaptic input/integrative processing) more closely than multi-unit spiking.

references.authors: Polimeni JR, Lewis LD
references.title: Imaging faster neural dynamics with fast fMRI: A need for updated models of the hemodynamic response
references.takeaway: Reviews fast-fMRI vascular physics and demonstrates why standard space- and time-invariant canonical HRF assumptions require revision at sub-second timescales.

lessons.technique: Hemodynamic response basis sets (canonical HRF, Taylor temporal/dispersion derivatives, and Finite Impulse Response deconvolution) and the bias-variance trade-off
lessons.why_it_matters: Hemodynamic onset and time-to-peak vary by 1–2.5 seconds across cortical regions, individuals, and age or vascular groups (Handwerker et al., 2004), so fitting a fixed canonical HRF template systematically underestimates true response amplitudes and leaves structured biphasic residuals when latency shifts occur. Augmenting the design matrix with Taylor derivative basis functions (Friston et al., 1998; Calhoun et al., 2004), voxel-wise empirical HRF libraries (GLMsingle; Prince et al., 2022), or multi-lag Finite Impulse Response (FIR) deconvolution models lets researchers trade controlled parameter variance against template misspecification bias.

references.authors: Friston K, Fletcher P, Josephs O, Holmes A, Rugg M, Turner R
references.title: Event-Related fMRI: Characterizing Differential Responses
references.takeaway: Introduces the canonical double-gamma HRF paired with its temporal derivative as a Taylor-expansion basis set to capture small latency differences in event-related fMRI.

references.authors: Handwerker DA, Ollinger JM, D'Esposito M
references.title: Variation of BOLD hemodynamic responses across subjects and brain regions and their effects on statistical analyses
references.takeaway: Empirically measures HRF time-to-peak variability across 20 subjects and four cortical regions, proving that 1–2.5 s onset/peak mismatches attenuate canonical GLM betas and cause false negatives.

references.authors: Lindquist MA, Meng Loh J, Atlas LY, Wager TD
references.title: Modeling the hemodynamic response function in fMRI: Efficiency, bias and mis-modeling
references.takeaway: Benchmarks canonical, derivative, smooth basis, and FIR HRF models with respect to estimation bias, variance, latency mis-modeling, and group-level inference power.

references.authors: Prince JS, Charest I, Kurzawski JW, Pyles JA, Tarr MJ, Kay KN
references.title: Improving the accuracy of single-trial fMRI response estimates using GLMsingle
references.takeaway: Introduces GLMsingle, combining voxel-wise selection from an empirical HRF library with data-driven denoising and ridge regularization to reduce HRF misspecification bias without FIR variance inflation.

lessons.technique: Contrast-specific GLM design efficiency, inter-stimulus interval (ISI) jittering, predictor collinearity, and regressor orthogonalization
lessons.why_it_matters: In task-fMRI general linear models, statistical precision for a scientific contrast c^T beta is governed by [c^T (X^T X)^{-1} c]^{-1}, meaning that the same schedule can differ tenfold in efficiency depending on whether the target contrast is a differential comparison (A - B) or a baseline sum (A + B). Designing schedules with rest blocks or exponentially jittered null events (Dale, 1999; Liu et al., 2001) and avoiding automatic Gram-Schmidt regressor orthogonalization (Mumford et al., 2015; Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020) prevents severe variance inflation and unintended changes to the tested parameter.

references.authors: Dale AM
references.title: Optimal experimental design for event-related fMRI
references.takeaway: Proves that jittering inter-stimulus intervals with null events decorrelates overlapping trial regressors and enables efficient deconvolution of rapid event-related fMRI responses.

references.authors: Liu TT, Frank LR, Wong EC, Buxton RB
references.title: Detection Power, Estimation Efficiency, and Predictability in Event-Related fMRI
references.takeaway: Derives the fundamental mathematical trade-off between detection power (maximized by blocked designs) and HRF estimation efficiency (maximized by randomized rapid event-related designs).

references.title: Orthogonalization of Regressors in fMRI Models
references.takeaway: Proves that Gram-Schmidt regressor orthogonalization in fMRI GLMs does not cure collinearity and instead redefines the scientific interpretation of the unorthogonalized regressor's parameter.

references.takeaway: Demonstrates across 70 analysis teams that failing to separate correlated parametric modulators from main task regressors in first-level fMRI design matrices alters the effective contrast and can invert group maps.

lessons.technique: Factorial experimental designs, treatment vs sum/effect contrast coding, multi-site cell-imbalance confounding, and direct interaction testing
lessons.why_it_matters: Neuroimaging studies routinely cross cognitive conditions, clinical diagnoses, and scanner sites in factorial designs to test modulation beyond simple cognitive subtraction (Friston et al., 1996). Misinterpreting dummy-coded coefficients as marginal main effects in the presence of an interaction (Schad et al., 2020), pooling unbalanced site-by-diagnosis cells without stratification or harmonization (Fortin et al., 2018), or claiming an interaction because one subgroup has p < 0.05 and another has p > 0.05—an error found in nearly half of surveyed neuroscience papers (Gelman & Stern, 2006; Nieuwenhuis et al., 2011)—leads directly to false scientific conclusions.

references.authors: Friston K, Price C, Fletcher P, Moore C, Frackowiak R, Dolan R
references.title: The Trouble with Cognitive Subtraction
references.takeaway: Critiques the pure insertion assumption of cognitive subtraction and establishes factorial designs and explicit interaction contrasts as the rigorous alternative in neuroimaging.

references.authors: Gelman A, Stern H
references.title: The Difference Between “Significant” and “Not Significant” is not Itself Statistically Significant
references.takeaway: Demonstrates mathematically why observing p < 0.05 in one subgroup and p > 0.05 in another does not imply a statistically significant difference or interaction between them.

references.authors: Nieuwenhuis S, Forstmann BU, Wagenmakers E
references.title: Erroneous analyses of interactions in neuroscience: a problem of significance
references.takeaway: Audits 157 neuroscience papers and shows that nearly half (78/157) committed the difference-in-significance fallacy instead of computing the direct factorial interaction contrast.

references.authors: Schad DJ, Vasishth S, Hohenstein S, Kliegl R
references.title: How to capitalize on a priori contrasts in linear (mixed) models: A tutorial
references.takeaway: Provides a comprehensive mathematical tutorial on contrast coding matrices, showing why treatment/dummy coding yields simple effects while sum/effect coding recovers true marginal main effects in factorial models.

lessons.technique: General linear model (GLM) contrast specification, covariance propagation, and t/F/z inference
lessons.why_it_matters: Every mass-univariate fMRI analysis (in SPM, FSL FEAT, AFNI 3dDeconvolve, and nilearn) translates scientific hypotheses into linear contrast vectors c applied to GLM parameter estimates. Without explicit name-aligned contrast vectors and full covariance propagation c^T (X^T X)^{-1} c, column permutations silently test the wrong scientific comparison and positive predictor correlation causes naive variance formulas to underestimate standard errors. Reporting both physical-unit effect estimates (COPE/VARCOPE) and test statistics prevents thresholded z-maps from hiding small-sample effect inflation or inter-pipeline agreement (Chen et al., 2017; Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020; Taylor et al., 2023).

references.authors: Friston KJ, Holmes AP, Worsley KJ, Poline J, Frith CD, Frackowiak RSJ
references.title: Statistical parametric maps in functional imaging: A general linear approach
references.takeaway: Introduces the statistical parametric mapping (SPM) general linear model framework and voxelwise t/F contrast inference.

references.authors: Poline J, Brett M
references.title: The general linear model and fMRI: Does love last forever?
references.takeaway: Explains the mathematical foundations, history, and common pitfalls of the GLM and contrast specification in fMRI.

references.authors: Chen G, Taylor PA, Cox RW
references.title: Is the statistic value all we should care about in neuroimaging?
references.takeaway: Demonstrates why reporting only dimensionless t/z statistics without physical-unit effect estimates (c^T beta_hat) distorts scientific interpretation.

references.authors: Taylor PA, Reynolds RC, Calhoun V, Gonzalez-Castillo J, Handwerker DA, Bandettini PA et al.
references.title: Highlight results, don't hide them: Enhance interpretation, reduce biases and improve reproducibility
references.takeaway: Shows that transparent reporting of unthresholded effect and statistic maps improves reproducibility and reveals agreement masked by binary thresholding.

lessons.technique: fMRI temporal autocorrelation modeling, prewhitening, and generalized least squares (GLS)
lessons.why_it_matters: First-level fMRI time series exhibit strong positive autocorrelation from slow hemodynamic sluggishness, physiological pulsations, and scanner drift (Purdon & Weisskoff, 1998; Woolrich et al., 2001). Applying ordinary least squares (OLS) without prewhitening underestimates the standard error of slow task designs by several fold, inflating first-level false-positive rates (Eklund et al., 2012; Olszowy et al., 2019). Valid inference requires symmetrical Cholesky prewhitening of both the data y and the design matrix X using an expressive noise covariance model (such as SPM FAST or AFNI 3dREMLfit ARMA(1,1) at short multiband TRs; Corbin et al., 2018; Olszowy et al., 2019).

references.authors: Purdon PL, Weisskoff RM
references.title: Effect of temporal autocorrelation due to physiological noise and stimulus paradigm on voxel-level false-positive rates in fMRI
references.takeaway: Establishes how physiological noise and temporal autocorrelation inflate voxel-level false-positive rates in fMRI when unmodeled.

references.authors: Woolrich MW, Ripley BD, Brady M, Smith SM
references.title: Temporal Autocorrelation in Univariate Linear Modeling of FMRI Data
references.takeaway: Introduces FSL FILM prewhitening via Tukey-tapered, spatially smoothed autocorrelation estimation for valid GLS inference in fMRI.

references.authors: Corbin N, Todd N, Friston KJ, Callaghan MF
references.title: Accurate modeling of temporal correlations in rapidly sampled fMRI time series
references.takeaway: Evaluates high-order AR (SPM FAST) and autocorrelation models for rapidly sampled multiband fMRI time series.

references.authors: Olszowy W, Aston J, Rua C, Williams GB
references.title: Accurate autocorrelation modeling substantially improves fMRI reliability
references.takeaway: Benchmarks SPM, FSL, and AFNI autocorrelation models across resting-state and task datasets, showing AFNI 3dREMLfit and SPM FAST best control false positives at short TRs.

lessons.technique: Multilevel mixed-effects modeling, repeated-measures hierarchy, and empirical Bayes shrinkage
lessons.why_it_matters: Neuroimaging datasets are inherently hierarchical, nesting trials within runs, runs within participants, and participants within scanner sites (Beckmann et al., 2003; Woolrich et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2012). Treating repeated runs as independent observations (pseudoreplication; Lazic, 2010) divides variance by N*R instead of N and severely inflates false-positive rates, while scrambling participant IDs in longitudinal contrasts destroys within-subject variance cancellation. Propagating first-level error variances (VARCOPEs) into second-level mixed-effects models (FSL FLAME, AFNI 3dMEMA) and balancing sample size N against scan duration R (Chen et al., 2022; Marek et al., 2022; Kang et al., 2024) are essential for replicable group inference.

references.authors: Beckmann CF, Jenkinson M, Smith SM
references.title: General multilevel linear modeling for group analysis in FMRI
references.takeaway: Derives the general multilevel linear model for fMRI group analysis separating within-subject and between-subject variance components.

references.authors: Woolrich MW, Behrens TE, Beckmann CF, Jenkinson M, Smith SM
references.title: Multilevel linear modelling for FMRI group analysis using Bayesian inference
references.takeaway: Introduces FSL FLAME multilevel Bayesian inference propagating first-level error variances into group-level fMRI analysis.

references.authors: Lazic SE
references.title: The problem of pseudoreplication in neuroscientific studies: is it affecting your analysis?
references.takeaway: Demonstrates how pooling repeated measurements per subject without hierarchical modeling causes pseudoreplication and inflated false positives in neuroscience.

references.authors: Chen G, Pine DS, Brotman MA, Smith AR, Cox RW, Taylor PA et al.
references.title: Hyperbolic trade-off: The importance of balancing trial and subject sample sizes in neuroimaging
references.takeaway: Quantifies the hyperbolic trade-off between trial/run count R and participant sample size N in hierarchical neuroimaging precision.

lessons.technique: Nonparametric permutation inference, exchangeability blocks, and cluster/subject bootstrap resampling
lessons.why_it_matters: When Gaussian random field assumptions fail in neuroimaging, nonparametric permutation tests (in FSL randomise and PALM) provide exact or conservative false-positive control—provided the rearranged configurations are exchangeable under the null hypothesis (Nichols & Holmes, 2002; Winkler et al., 2014). Shuffling rows across repeated runs, twin families, or scanner sites violates exchangeability (requiring multi-level block permutation; Winkler et al., 2015), and omitting the +1 identity count in Monte Carlo permutation p-values yields invalid p = 0 claims (Phipson & Smyth, 2010). Likewise, bootstrap resampling must resample independent participants rather than flat rows and does not make the sample mean robust to extreme outliers.

references.authors: Nichols TE, Holmes AP
references.title: Nonparametric permutation tests for functional neuroimaging: A primer with examples
references.takeaway: Establishes the nonparametric permutation testing framework and exchangeability principles for functional neuroimaging.

references.authors: Phipson B, Smyth GK
references.title: Permutation P-values Should Never Be Zero: Calculating Exact P-values When Permutations Are Randomly Drawn
references.venue: Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular Biology
references.takeaway: Proves that Monte Carlo permutation p-values must include the observed configuration (+1 in numerator and denominator) to preserve valid Type I error control.

references.authors: Winkler AM, Ridgway GR, Webster MA, Smith SM, Nichols TE
references.title: Permutation inference for the general linear model
references.takeaway: Provides the definitive formulation of permutation inference for the GLM, including Freedman-Lane nuisance residualization and exchangeability blocks in FSL randomise/PALM.

references.authors: Winkler AM, Renaud O, Smith SM, Nichols TE
references.title: Permutation inference for canonical correlation analysis
references.takeaway: Extends block-exchangeable and nuisance-adjusted permutation inference to multivariate canonical correlation analysis in large neuroimaging cohorts.

lessons.technique: Multiple comparisons control: family-wise error rate (FWER), false discovery rate (FDR), random field theory (RFT), and threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE)
lessons.why_it_matters: Whole-brain neuroimaging tests 50,000–200,000 voxels simultaneously, guaranteeing dozens of false positives per map under uncorrected thresholding. Choosing between voxelwise FWER, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (Genovese et al., 2002), cluster-extent thresholding (Worsley et al., 1996; Woo et al., 2014), and TFCE (Smith & Nichols, 2009) changes both the controlled error criterion and the spatial unit of inference. Because empirical fMRI spatial autocorrelation has heavier tails than a Gaussian kernel, parametric cluster-extent RFT at lenient thresholds (p < 0.01) inflates FWER up to ~70% (Eklund et al., 2016), making permutation-calibrated max-statistic or TFCE inference essential.

references.authors: Worsley KJ, Marrett S, Neelin P, Vandal AC, Friston KJ, Evans AC
references.title: A unified statistical approach for determining significant signals in images of cerebral activation
references.takeaway: Formulates unified Gaussian random field (RFT) theory for voxelwise and cluster-extent family-wise error control in neuroimaging.

references.authors: Genovese CR, Lazar NA, Nichols T
references.title: Thresholding of Statistical Maps in Functional Neuroimaging Using the False Discovery Rate
references.takeaway: Introduces False Discovery Rate (FDR) thresholding to functional neuroimaging as an adaptive alternative to FWER.

references.authors: SMITH S, NICHOLS T
references.title: Threshold-free cluster enhancement: Addressing problems of smoothing, threshold dependence and localisation in cluster inference
references.takeaway: Introduces Threshold-Free Cluster Enhancement (TFCE), integrating cluster extent and height across thresholds without an arbitrary cluster-forming cutoff.

references.authors: Noble S, Scheinost D, Constable RT
references.title: Cluster failure or power failure? Evaluating sensitivity in cluster-level inference
references.takeaway: Evaluates sensitivity and power trade-offs of cluster-level and TFCE inference under stringent FWER control in modern fMRI cohorts.

lessons.technique: Circular analysis (double dipping) detection, winner's curse bias, and independent ROI validation
lessons.why_it_matters: Selecting regions of interest (ROIs) or voxels using the same data—or a statistically dependent contrast—later used to estimate effect sizes or p-values conditions the test statistic on passing a selection threshold, inflating effect estimates via the winner's curse and invalidating inference (Kriegeskorte et al., 2009; Vul et al., 2009). Avoiding circularity requires anatomical priors, independent functional localizer runs (Saxe et al., 2006; Poldrack, 2007), leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (Esterman et al., 2010), or outer-loop split-sample isolation in machine learning pipelines (Rosenblatt et al., 2024). Even within a single GLM run, orthogonal contrast weights are insufficient for independence unless design and noise covariance matrices yield zero estimator covariance.

references.authors: Saxe R, Brett M, Kanwisher N
references.title: Divide and conquer: A defense of functional localizers
references.takeaway: Establishes the methodology and rationale for independent functional localizer scans in region-of-interest fMRI studies.

references.authors: Poldrack RA
references.title: Region of interest analysis for fMRI
references.takeaway: Provides best-practice guidelines for ROI definition, anatomical vs. functional localization, and avoiding selection bias in fMRI.

references.authors: Vul E, Harris C, Winkielman P, Pashler H
references.title: Puzzlingly High Correlations in fMRI Studies of Emotion, Personality, and Social Cognition
references.takeaway: Demonstrates how non-independent voxel selection produced inflated brain-behavior correlations across the social cognitive neuroscience literature.

references.authors: Rosenblatt M, Tejavibulya L, Jiang R, Noble S, Scheinost D
references.title: Data leakage inflates prediction performance in connectome-based machine learning models
references.takeaway: Quantifies how feature-selection, harmonization, and hyperparameter data leakage inflate connectome-based machine learning performance across large neuroimaging cohorts.

lessons.technique: Effect-size estimation, frequentist confidence intervals, conjugate Bayesian updating, and TOST/ROPE equivalence testing
lessons.why_it_matters: A non-significant p-value (p > 0.05) never proves the absence of an effect; it fails to distinguish a genuinely negligible effect from a noisy, underpowered study (Altman & Bland, 1995; Lakens, 2017). Conversely, in large neuroimaging cohorts (N > 1,000), tiny, practically trivial effects routinely reach p < 0.05. Distinguishing statistical significance from practical importance requires reporting physical-unit effect estimates with confidence or credible intervals (Morey et al., 2016) and testing against a prespecified smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) via Two One-Sided Tests (TOST; Schuirmann, 1987; Lakens, 2018) or Bayesian Region of Practical Equivalence (ROPE; Kruschke, 2018; Linde et al., 2023).

references.authors: Schuirmann DJ
references.title: A comparison of the Two One-Sided Tests Procedure and the Power Approach for assessing the equivalence of average bioavailability
references.takeaway: Establishes the Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) procedure and its operational equivalence to the (1 - 2*alpha) confidence interval inclusion rule.

references.title: Equivalence Testing for Psychological Research: A Tutorial
references.venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
references.takeaway: Provides a comprehensive tutorial on choosing smallest effect sizes of interest (SESOI) and combining NHST with TOST equivalence testing.

references.title: Rejecting or Accepting Parameter Values in Bayesian Estimation
references.venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
references.takeaway: Formulates the Bayesian Highest Density Interval + Region of Practical Equivalence (HDI-ROPE) decision rule and compares it with frequentist TOST.

references.authors: Linde M, Tendeiro JN, Selker R, Wagenmakers E, van Ravenzwaaij D
references.title: Decisions about equivalence: A comparison of TOST, HDI-ROPE, and the Bayes factor.
references.takeaway: Systematically compares TOST, Bayesian HDI-ROPE, and Bayes factor equivalence procedures across sample sizes and prior specifications.

lessons.technique: Multiverse analysis, specification curves, causal covariate selection, preregistration, and cryptographic provenance
lessons.why_it_matters: Modern neuroimaging pipelines involve dozens of defensible preprocessing, quality-control, and statistical modeling choices—the 'garden of forking paths' (Carp, 2012; Gelman & Loken, 2014; Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020). Selectively reporting the single pipeline that yields p < 0.05 severely inflates false discoveries (Simmons et al., 2011). Preregistration (Nosek et al., 2018), multiverse and specification-curve analysis across causally justified analytic branches (Steegen et al., 2016; Simonsohn et al., 2020; Dafflon et al., 2022), and cryptographic input/environment provenance (Poldrack et al., 2017) separate robust scientific effects from pipeline-fragile artifacts and collider/confounder bias.

references.title: On the Plurality of (Methodological) Worlds: Estimating the Analytic Flexibility of fMRI Experiments
references.takeaway: Quantifies the vast analytic flexibility across thousands of fMRI pipeline combinations and its impact on spatial activation maps.

references.title: Increasing Transparency Through a Multiverse Analysis
references.takeaway: Introduces multiverse analysis for evaluating how arbitrary data-processing and modeling choices affect scientific conclusions.

references.title: Specification curve analysis
references.takeaway: Formulates specification curve analysis for visualizing and conducting joint inference across theoretically justified analytical specifications.

references.title: A guided multiverse study of neuroimaging analyses
references.takeaway: Applies guided multiverse analysis to neuroimaging pipelines to map decision sensitivity and robustness across model spaces.

lessons.technique: 4D neuroimaging array shapes, strided memory layout, axis reductions, and reversible 2D brain-mask flattening
lessons.why_it_matters: Every fMRI and dMRI pipeline (fMRIPrep, Nilearn NiftiMasker, FSL, Connectome Workbench) converts between 4D spatial volumes (X, Y, Z, T) and 2D sample-by-feature matrices (T, V_in-brain). Confusing C-contiguous (row-major) and Fortran-contiguous (column-major) reshape orders, omitting keepdims=True when broadcasting temporal summaries, or applying scikit-learn transformers to transposed (V, T) matrices silently scrambles voxel anatomy while preserving matrix shape and global summary statistics.

lessons.technique: Tidy relational tables, BIDS multi-level key joins, and participant-grouped cross-validation
lessons.why_it_matters: Neuroimaging datasets in BIDS format store demographics at the participant level, clinical visits at the session level, and QC metrics at the scan-run level. Careless inner/many-to-many joins silently drop participants or duplicate rows, and splitting at the scan-run level (KFold) rather than the participant level (GroupKFold) leaks individual connectome fingerprints across train and test folds, producing severely inflated predictive R^2.

lessons.technique: NIfTI-1 binary headers, voxel-to-world RAS+ affine transforms, and scl_slope/scl_inter integer quantization
lessons.why_it_matters: Every volumetric MRI file pairs a raw voxel array with a 348-byte NIfTI-1 header encoding the 4x4 voxel-to-world affine matrix (qform/sform) and linear intensity scaling (scl_slope, scl_inter). Casting floating-point statistical maps to int16 without header scaling truncates sub-unit effect sizes to zero, while overwriting the header affine with an identity matrix destroys physical millimeter geometry and hemisphere orientation in downstream tools like fMRIPrep, FSL, and ANTs.

lessons.technique: Robust location/scale estimators (median, IQR, MAD), breakdown points, and outlier-resistant neuroimaging QC
lessons.why_it_matters: Neuroimaging quality metrics (framewise displacement, DVARS, tSNR) and multi-site morphometry exhibit heavy right skew, coil-artifact spikes, and scanner bimodality. Because the sample mean and standard deviation have a 0% asymptotic breakdown point, even a few extreme motion spikes inflate the SD and mask moderate artifacts under Z-score thresholding, whereas median/MAD (50% breakdown) and IQR (25% breakdown) provide stable quality-control thresholds in pipelines such as MRIQC and fMRIPrep.

lessons.technique: Missing-data mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR), motion-QC attrition bias, and fold-isolated imputation pipelines
lessons.why_it_matters: Excluding high-motion scans or incomplete clinical visits does not remove data at random: head motion correlates with age and symptom severity, inducing Missing at Random (MAR) or Missing Not at Random (MNAR) selection bias in complete-case analyses (Nebel et al., 2022). Furthermore, imputing missing features across the full dataset or conditioning on the outcome before cross-validation leaks test-fold information and fabricates predictive signal on pure noise (Kapoor & Narayanan, 2023).

lessons.technique: Bayesian inverse probability, base-rate fallacy, positive predictive value (PPV), and prior-shift log-odds calibration
lessons.why_it_matters: Neuroimaging classifiers and foundation models (such as BrainIAC) are frequently trained on balanced 1:1 case-control cohorts (50% prevalence) but deployed in clinical screening or population biobanks where true disease prevalence is 1-2%. Without Bayes' rule prior-shift recalibration (Saerens et al., 2002), a classifier with 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity yields a positive predictive value below 16% at 2% prevalence, turning over 84% of positive flags into false alarms.

references.authors: Saerens M, Latinne P, Decaestecker C
references.title: Adjusting the Outputs of a Classifier to New a Priori Probabilities: A Simple Procedure

references.takeaway: Establishes clinical probability calibration diagnostics and demonstrates how miscalibrated risk scores lead to harmful decision-threshold errors under prevalence shift.

lessons.technique: Sampling variability, Kish's clustered design effect (DEFF) and effective sample size, and Type M / Type S errors
lessons.why_it_matters: Brain-wide association studies (BWAS) typically target small true correlations (|r| ~ 0.05-0.15) using multi-site or family-clustered cohorts (ABCD, HCP, UK Biobank). At small sample sizes (N = 25), significance filtering guarantees at least a 3.96x magnitude exaggeration (Type M error / winner's curse) and ~10% sign flips (Type S error), while ignoring within-participant or twin intraclass correlation (ICC) inflates naive false-positive rates from 5% tonearly 29%.

references.authors: Gelman A, Carlin J
references.title: Beyond Power Calculations
