lessons.technique: Nonparametric and participant-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals, out-of-bag (OOB) leakage, and bootstrap stability selection
lessons.why_it_matters: Bootstrap resampling provides distribution-free confidence intervals and feature-selection stability metrics across skewed neuroimaging phenotypes and high-dimensional connectomes (Marek et al., 2022; Rousselet et al., 2021). However, resampling individual scan rows rather than participant clusters shrinks confidence intervals by 1/sqrt(DEFF) and causes ~98.2% of out-of-bag scans (with m=5 scans/subject) to have sibling scans from the same participant in-bag, invalidating out-of-bag generalization estimates.

references.authors: Efron B
references.title: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife
references.takeaway: Introduces the nonparametric bootstrap plug-in principle for estimating sampling distributions and confidence intervals via resampling with replacement.

references.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology
references.takeaway: Establishes the theoretical properties of the cluster bootstrap, showing that resampling must occur at the independent cluster (participant) level to preserve variance calibration.

references.authors: Meinshausen N, Bühlmann P
references.title: Stability Selection

references.takeaway: Formalizes stability selection via subsampling/bootstrap inclusion probabilities to separate reproducible sparse features from high-dimensional noise.

references.venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
references.takeaway: Provides a modern tutorial on percentile bootstrap confidence intervals for skewed and heteroscedastic neuroscience and behavioral data.

lessons.technique: Feature scaling, baseline normalization (percent signal change), and temporal vs. spatial standardization
lessons.why_it_matters: Every fMRI pipeline (AFNI afni_proc.py, FSL FEAT, SPM, nilearn) requires choosing how raw scanner intensities are scaled before regression or multivariate decoding. Dividing by baseline equilibrium magnetization converts arbitrary scanner units into physical percent signal change (PSC) that cancels multiplicative coil gain, whereas temporal z-scoring divides by the total time-series standard deviation and confounds true neural response amplitude with thermal and physiological noise (Chen et al., 2017; Welvaert & Rosseel, 2013). Standardization choices also determine the reference axis (temporal axis=0 vs. spatial axis=1) and baseline definition (rest-period vs. whole-run mean), which directly alter effect-size magnitudes across regions and cohorts.

references.authors: Chen G, Taylor PA, Cox RW
references.title: Is the statistic value all we should care about in neuroimaging?
references.takeaway: Demonstrates why fMRI effect estimates should be reported in physical units (percent signal change) alongside dimensionless test statistics so response amplitude is not confounded with noise.

references.authors: Welvaert M, Rosseel Y
references.title: On the Definition of Signal-To-Noise Ratio and Contrast-To-Noise Ratio for fMRI Data
references.takeaway: Formalizes the definitions of fMRI signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), clarifying how temporal z-scoring converts effect amplitudes into CNR-weighted quantities.

references.takeaway: Reviews common misconceptions in applying the GLM to fMRI, including grand-mean vs. voxelwise baseline scaling and percent signal change interpretation.

references.title: Processing, evaluating, and understanding FMRI data with afni_proc.py
references.takeaway: Details modern fMRI preprocessing and scaling conventions in afni_proc.py, including voxelwise mean normalization to percent signal change and quality-control diagnostics.

lessons.technique: Linear algebra of the General Linear Model: column space projection, rank deficiency, contrast estimability, and Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse
lessons.why_it_matters: Neuroimaging GLMs (SPM, FSL FEAT, AFNI 3dDeconvolve, nilearn) routinely encounter rank-deficient or nearly collinear design matrices from overspecified dummy variables, multi-site covariates, or rapid event-related trials convolved with the sluggish hemodynamic response. Understanding column-space projection P = X X+, the rank-nullity theorem, and the contrast estimability condition c in R(X^T) explains why fitted predictions y_hat are invariant to the generalized inverse even when individual beta_hat coordinates are non-unique, and why collinear regressors inflate contrast variance Var(c^T beta_hat) = sigma^2 c^T (X^T X)^-1 c and collapse test-retest reliability (Smith et al., 2007; Prince et al., 2022).

references.authors: Penrose R
references.title: A generalized inverse for matrices
references.venue: Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society
references.takeaway: Establishes the existence and uniqueness of the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse X+ via the four Penrose conditions, providing the minimum-norm least-squares solution for rank-deficient design matrices.

references.authors: Smith S, Jenkinson M, Beckmann C, Miller K, Woolrich M
references.title: Meaningful design and contrast estimability in FMRI
references.takeaway: Defines meaningful contrast specification, estimability, and design efficiency (1 / c^T (X^T X)^-1 c) for fMRI general linear models.

references.authors: Mumford JA, Poline J, Poldrack RA
references.title: Orthogonalization of Regressors in fMRI Models
references.takeaway: Shows how collinearity operates in fMRI design matrices and why sequential regressor orthogonalization alters parameter interpretation without changing the overall subspace projection.

references.authors: Prince JS, Charest I, Kurzawski JW, Pyles JA, Tarr MJ, Kay KN
references.title: Improving the accuracy of single-trial fMRI response estimates using GLMsingle
references.takeaway: Introduces GLMsingle to stabilize single-trial fMRI beta estimates under severe hemodynamic collinearity using library HRFs, GLMdenoise, and fractional ridge regression.

lessons.technique: Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), loss-function equivalence, robust M-estimation (L1/Huber/Student-t), and AIC/BIC model selection
lessons.why_it_matters: Choosing a loss function in neuroimaging regression or time-series modeling implicitly specifies a probability distribution for the noise via maximum likelihood estimation. Because head-motion spikes, physiological bursts, and coil glitches generate heavy-tailed residuals, ordinary least squares (Gaussian MLE) suffers unbounded linear influence psi(r) = r/sigma^2, whereas Laplace (L1), Huber, and Student-t likelihoods bound or redescend outlier influence (Huber, 1964; Wager et al., 2005). Simultaneously, likelihood-based criteria (AIC, BIC, cross-validated deviance) are needed to select nuisance drift orders or hidden-state counts without overfitting noise.

references.authors: Huber PJ
references.title: Robust Estimation of a Location Parameter
references.takeaway: Introduces M-estimation and Huber's loss function, bounding the influence function of extreme residuals to bridge quadratic (L2) and absolute-error (L1) estimation.

references.authors: Akaike H
references.title: A new look at the statistical model identification
references.takeaway: Establishes the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC = 2k - 2 ln L) from Kullback-Leibler divergence to penalize model complexity when comparing maximum-likelihood fits.

references.authors: Wager TD, Keller MC, Lacey SC, Jonides J
references.title: Increased sensitivity in neuroimaging analyses using robust regression
references.takeaway: Demonstrates that iteratively reweighted least-squares (IRLS) robust regression suppresses outlier artifacts and increases statistical sensitivity in neuroimaging group analyses.

references.authors: Olszowy W, Aston J, Rua C, Williams GB
references.title: Accurate autocorrelation modeling substantially improves fMRI reliability
references.takeaway: Evaluates fMRI noise and autocorrelation models across software packages, showing how misspecified noise likelihoods inflate false positives and degrade reliability.

lessons.technique: Numerical optimization, Hessian conditioning, Polyak momentum, spectral stability bounds, and local minima vs. closed-form keypoint alignment
lessons.why_it_matters: Classical anatomical and functional image registration tools (FSL FLIRT/FNIRT, ANTs SyN, SPM coregistration) as well as deep neuroimaging models minimize non-convex objectives with ill-conditioned Hessians where rotational and translational parameters differ in curvature by orders of magnitude. Understanding step-size stability bounds (eta < 2 / lambda_max), condition-number contraction rates, momentum damping (Polyak, 1964), and multi-resolution or keypoint-based closed-form solvers (Jenkinson et al., 2002; Balakrishnan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025) explains why naive gradient descent oscillates, diverges, or traps in false sulcal local minima.

references.authors: Polyak B
references.title: Some methods of speeding up the convergence of iteration methods
references.venue: USSR Computational Mathematics and Mathematical Physics
references.takeaway: Introduces the heavy-ball momentum method and proves via spectral analysis how momentum reduces the effective condition-number dependence from kappa to sqrt(kappa).

references.authors: Jenkinson M, Bannister P, Brady M, Smith S
references.title: Improved Optimization for the Robust and Accurate Linear Registration and Motion Correction of Brain Images
references.takeaway: Analyzes the non-convex optimization landscape and local minima of 3D brain image registration, introducing the multi-resolution global search strategy used in FSL FLIRT.

references.authors: Bottou L, Curtis FE, Nocedal J
references.title: Optimization Methods for Large-Scale Machine Learning
references.takeaway: Provides a comprehensive mathematical review of first-order, momentum, adaptive, and second-order preconditioned optimization methods in machine learning.

references.authors: Balakrishnan G, Zhao A, Sabuncu MR, Guttag J, Dalca AV
references.title: VoxelMorph: A Learning Framework for Deformable Medical Image Registration
references.takeaway: Replaces costly per-pair iterative image registration optimization with an amortized convolutional network (VoxelMorph) trained across a population of brain volumes.

lessons.technique: Regression diagnostics: hat-matrix leverage, studentized residuals, Cook's distance, Sherman-Morrison LOO deletion, and Variance Inflation Factors (VIF)
lessons.why_it_matters: Brain-behavior and morphometric regressions frequently combine modest sample sizes with heavy-tailed motion or segmentation outliers and highly correlated bilateral or multi-site predictors. A single high-leverage outlier can invert an ordinary least-squares slope and manufacture a false p < 0.01 discovery (Cook, 1977; Rousselet & Pernet, 2012), while high predictor collinearity (large VIF) inflates standard errors and causes erratic sign flips across homologous regions. Auditing leverage h_ii, Cook's distance D_i, VIF, and residual structure before reporting p-values prevents fragile or misspecified claims.

references.authors: Cook RD
references.title: Detection of Influential Observation in Linear Regression
references.takeaway: Derives Cook's distance D_i combining studentized residuals and hat-matrix leverage h_ii to quantify how deleting a single observation shifts the fitted regression vector.

references.authors: Rousselet GA, Pernet CR
references.title: Improving standards in brain-behavior correlation analyses
references.takeaway: Shows how high-leverage outliers distort ordinary least-squares and Pearson brain-behavior correlations in small neuroimaging samples and advocates robust diagnostics.

references.title: An Updated Guide to Robust Statistical Methods in Neuroscience
references.takeaway: Provides an updated methodological guide to outlier detection, leverage diagnostics, and robust statistical estimation in neuroscience.

references.title: Study design features increase replicability in brain-wide association studies
references.takeaway: Demonstrates how predictor variance spread and study design features govern effect-size stability and replicability in brain-wide association regressions.

lessons.technique: Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), Eckart-Young low-rank approximation, and unsupervised variance vs. supervised signal
lessons.why_it_matters: PCA and SVD underpin functional connectivity eigenmodes, ICA pre-whitening (FSL MELODIC), representational similarity analysis (PM02), and feature compression prior to clinical prediction. Because SVD orders components purely by unsupervised variance sigma_k^2 / sum(sigma_j^2), global nuisance fluctuations (scanner drift, head size, physiological noise) often dominate the leading PCs while focal clinical or cognitive signals reside in lower-variance components (Jolliffe, 1982). Furthermore, failing to mean-center features before SVD or fitting the PCA basis on pooled train+test data corrupts the subspace and leaks test geometry.

references.authors: Eckart C, Young G
references.title: The Approximation of One Matrix by Another of Lower Rank
references.takeaway: Proves that truncating the singular value decomposition at rank K yields the optimal rank-K matrix approximation under the Frobenius norm.

references.authors: Jolliffe IT
references.title: A Note on the Use of Principal Components in Regression
references.takeaway: Refutes the assumption that low-variance principal components are uninformative in regression, showing with real examples that trailing PCs can carry the primary predictive signal.

references.authors: Jolliffe IT, Cadima J
references.title: Principal component analysis: a review and recent developments
references.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences
references.takeaway: Reviews the linear algebra, centering requirements, geometric interpretation, and modern high-dimensional extensions of PCA and SVD.

references.authors: Vos de Wael R, Benkarim O, Paquola C, Lariviere S, Royer J, Tavakol S, et al.
references.title: BrainSpace: a toolbox for the analysis of macroscale gradients in neuroimaging and connectomics datasets
references.takeaway: Presents BrainSpace for computing PCA, SVD, and manifold gradients on high-dimensional neuroimaging and connectomics matrices.

lessons.technique: Cross-validation hygiene, feature-selection data leakage (double dipping), extreme-value order statistics, and full-pipeline permutation testing
lessons.why_it_matters: In high-dimensional neuroimaging matrices where features vastly outnumber participants (P >> N, such as 35,778 connectome edges in PM07 or >200,000 voxels in PD04), extreme-value statistics guarantee that pure Gaussian noise contains features with large sample correlations. Screening features, fitting PCA, or harmonizing covariates on the full dataset before cross-validation leaks test-fold labels into feature selection and fabricates high apparent R^2 and classification accuracy from noise (Ambroise & McLachlan, 2002; Kriegeskorte et al., 2009; Rosenblatt et al., 2024). Enforcing fold-isolated Pipeline objects and full-pipeline permutation testing is essential for valid out-of-sample inference.

references.authors: Ambroise C, McLachlan GJ
references.title: Selection bias in gene extraction on the basis of microarray gene-expression data
references.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
references.takeaway: Establishes that performing feature selection across all samples before cross-validation creates severe optimistic selection bias, requiring feature screening strictly inside each CV fold.

references.authors: Varoquaux G
references.title: Cross-validation failure: Small sample sizes lead to large error bars
references.takeaway: Quantifies the large sampling error bars of cross-validated accuracy in small-sample neuroimaging studies and explains how analytical choices inflate apparent performance.

references.title: Establishment of Best Practices for Evidence for Prediction
references.takeaway: Establishes best-practice standards for predictive modeling in neuroimaging and psychiatry, including nested cross-validation, fold isolation, and permutation testing.

references.authors: Rosenblatt M, Tejavibulya L, Jiang R, Noble S, Scheinost D
references.title: Data leakage inflates prediction performance in connectome-based machine learning models
references.takeaway: Systematically evaluates forms of data leakage (feature selection, covariate harmonization, subject-level splitting) in connectome-based neuroimaging prediction models.

lessons.technique: Computational reproducibility, cryptographic data provenance (SHA-256), IEEE-754 floating-point non-associativity, and specification curve analysis
lessons.why_it_matters: Even when 70 neuroimaging teams analyze the exact same dataset (Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020, PD01), silent data mutations, untracked software environments, floating-point summation differences, and legitimate analytical flexibility across preprocessing and modeling choices produce divergent conclusions. Combining containerized workflow provenance (Esteban et al., 2019, PP01; Gorgolewski et al., 2016), cryptographic input/output hashing, automated fold-hygiene verification, and specification curve analysis (Simonsohn et al., 2020) separates software bugs and data leakage from genuine analytical sensitivity.

references.authors: Sandve GK, Nekrutenko A, Taylor J, Hovig E
references.title: Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research
references.takeaway: Articulates ten foundational rules for reproducible computational research, covering version tracking, seed recording, intermediate data provenance, and automated execution.

references.title: The brain imaging data structure, a format for organizing and describing outputs of neuroimaging experiments
references.takeaway: Introduces the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) standard that enables automated, auditable, and reproducible neuroimaging workflows across laboratories.

references.authors: Simonsohn U, Simmons JP, Nelson LD
references.title: Specification curve analysis
references.takeaway: Formalizes specification curve analysis to quantify how effect estimates vary across the combinatorial space of defensible analytical choices.

references.authors: Bowring A, Maumet C, Nichols TE
references.title: Exploring the impact of analysis software on task fMRI results
references.takeaway: Demonstrates how executing equivalent task-fMRI pipelines across AFNI, FSL, and SPM yields systematic differences in statistical maps even on identical input data.

lessons.technique: Multivariate representations, forward encoding models, backward decoding models, and Haufe activation pattern recovery
lessons.why_it_matters: Encoding and decoding models form the core bridge between computational feature spaces (such as language embeddings, vision backbones, and task parameters) and distributed multi-voxel brain activity in modern fMRI and electrophysiology pipelines (e.g., Nilearn, BrainIAK, himalaya, and natural-scene reconstruction frameworks like MindEye2). Without distinguishing forward encoding parameters from backward discriminative weights, researchers routinely misinterpret noise-suppressing decoder channels as neural tuning (Haufe et al., 2014) or mistake coarse ROI averaging for absence of fine-grained columnar information. Mastering both directions forces explicit choices about regularization regime, sample-budget calibration, and covariance projection before making localization or representational claims.

references.authors: Haxby JV, Gobbini MI, Furey ML, Ishai A, Schouten JL, Pietrini P
references.title: Distributed and Overlapping Representations of Faces and Objects in Ventral Temporal Cortex
references.takeaway: Introduces distributed multi-voxel pattern analysis in ventral temporal cortex, showing category information survives outside maximally selective single voxels.

references.takeaway: Clarifies the causal and representational interpretation limits of encoding and decoding models in cognitive neuroscience.

lessons.technique: Regularized linear models (Ridge L2, Lasso L1, Elastic Net, and regularized logistic probing) under collinearity
lessons.why_it_matters: High-dimensional neuroimaging regressions—from voxelwise encoding (himalaya, Nilearn) to connectome-wide prediction and linear probing of foundation models (BrainIAC)—routinely operate in the p >> N regime with spatially correlated voxels. Without appropriate L2 or Elastic Net regularization, ordinary least squares suffers severe variance inflation along near-collinear dipole directions, while pure L1 (Lasso) arbitrarily drops correlated partner voxels across bootstrap resamples (Zou & Hastie, 2005). Understanding penalty geometry and singular-value shrinkage forces principled choices between dense distributed shrinkage (Ridge/banded Ridge) and grouped sparse selection (Elastic Net) inside fold-safe scaling pipelines.

references.authors: Hoerl AE, Kennard RW
references.title: Ridge Regression: Biased Estimation for Nonorthogonal Problems
references.takeaway: Introduces ridge regression and proves that adding a positive diagonal penalty trades a small bias for a large reduction in estimator variance under collinearity.

references.authors: Tibshirani R
references.title: Regression Shrinkage and Selection Via the Lasso
references.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology
references.takeaway: Introduces the L1-penalized Lasso estimator for simultaneous continuous shrinkage and exact variable selection.

references.authors: Zou H, Hastie T
references.title: Regularization and Variable Selection Via the Elastic Net
references.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology
references.takeaway: Combines L1 and L2 penalties in the Elastic Net to preserve sparsity while grouping correlated predictors instead of arbitrarily dropping all but one.

references.authors: Dupré la Tour T, Eickenberg M, Nunez-Elizalde AO, Gallant JL
references.title: Feature-space selection with banded ridge regression
references.takeaway: Demonstrates banded ridge regression for high-dimensional voxelwise encoding models with multiple correlated feature spaces.

lessons.technique: Kernel methods (RBF/linear SVMs), decision tree ensembles (Random Forests), and fair model-family comparison across dimensions
lessons.why_it_matters: Support vector machines and tree ensembles remain workhorse classifiers in MVPA, radiomics, and clinical neuroimaging benchmarks (scikit-learn, Nilearn), yet claims that nonlinear kernels or deep models outperform linear baselines frequently collapse when evaluation budgets and preprocessing are equalized (Schulz et al., 2020; He et al., 2020). In high-dimensional whole-brain spaces, unscreened noise features degrade isotropic RBF kernels toward random-gram memorization, while uncalibrated kernel bandwidths (gamma) either flatten into linear boundaries or overfit isolated support vectors. Mastering kernel geometry and ensemble variance reduction equips researchers to audit whether apparent model gains reflect true nonlinear structure or unequal hyperparameter tuning.

references.authors: Cortes C, Vapnik V
references.title: Support-vector networks
references.takeaway: Formulates maximum-margin support-vector networks and kernelized nonlinear decision boundaries via quadratic programming.

references.authors: Breiman L
references.title: Random Forests
references.takeaway: Introduces Random Forests, combining bootstrap aggregation and random feature subspacing to reduce variance in axis-aligned decision trees.

references.authors: Schulz M, Yeo BTT, Vogelstein JT, Mourao-Miranada J, Kather JN, Kording K, Richards B, Bzdok D
references.title: Different scaling of linear models and deep learning in UKBiobank brain images versus machine-learning datasets
references.takeaway: Shows across thousands of UK Biobank brain-imaging datasets that regularized linear models scale comparably to nonlinear kernels and deep networks for phenotype prediction.

references.authors: He T, Kong R, Holmes AJ, Nguyen M, Sabuncu MR, Eickhoff SB, Bzdok D, Feng J, Yeo BT
references.title: Deep neural networks and kernel regression achieve comparable accuracies for functional connectivity prediction of behavior and demographics
references.takeaway: Demonstrates that kernel ridge regression and deep neural networks achieve comparable accuracy when predicting behavior and demographics from functional connectomes under matched evaluation.

lessons.technique: Nested cross-validation, participant-grouped splitting (GroupKFold, LeaveOneGroupOut), and ComBat empirical Bayes site harmonization
lessons.why_it_matters: Multi-site consortia (ABCD, UK Biobank, ENIGMA, ADNI) combine scanners with distinct field-strength and vendor shifts alongside repeated longitudinal or twin observations. Splitting rows naively across folds leaks subject identity, tuning hyperparameters on outer test folds inflates generalization estimates (Varma & Simon, 2006), and applying ComBat harmonization (Johnson et al., 2007; Fortin et al., 2018) outside cross-validation or across site-confounded clinical cohorts either leaks test-site statistics or distorts biological variance (Nygaard et al., 2016). Enforcing participant-grouped nested splits and in-fold harmonization is essential for credible multi-site biomarker validation.

references.authors: Varma S, Simon R
references.title: Bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for model selection
references.takeaway: Demonstrates that tuning hyperparameters on the outer cross-validation test split induces substantial optimistic bias unless selection is isolated inside nested inner folds.

references.authors: Johnson WE, Li C, Rabinovic A
references.title: Adjusting batch effects in microarray expression data using empirical Bayes methods
references.takeaway: Introduces ComBat empirical Bayes location-and-scale batch harmonization, pooling information across features to stabilize small-site parameter estimates.

references.authors: Nygaard V, Rødland EA, Hovig E
references.title: Methods that remove batch effects while retaining group differences may lead to exaggerated confidence in downstream analyses
references.takeaway: Proves that batch-effect removal while retaining group covariates in unbalanced site-by-group designs can distort residual variance and inflate downstream confidence.

references.authors: Pomponio R, Erus G, Habes M, Doshi J, Srinivasan D, Mamourian E, Bashyam V, Nasrallah IM, Satterthwaite TD, Fan Y, Launer LJ, Masters CL, Maruff P, Zhuo C, Völzke H, Johnson SC, Fripp J, Koutsouleris N, Wolf DH, Gur R, Gur R, Morris J, Albert MS, Grabe HJ, Resnick SM, Bryan RN, Wolk DA, Shinohara RT, Shou H, Davatzikos C

references.takeaway: Extends ComBat with generalized additive models (ComBat-GAM / neuroHarmonize) to harmonize multi-site MRI measures while preserving nonlinear lifespan trajectories.

lessons.technique: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Independent Component Analysis (FastICA) for blind source separation
lessons.why_it_matters: PCA and ICA underpin spatial network discovery and artifact removal across fMRI and EEG/MEG pipelines, including FSL MELODIC (Beckmann & Smith, 2004), ICA-AROMA, GroupICA/NeuroMark (Du et al., 2020), and dimensionality reduction prior to state-space modeling. Because second-order covariance is invariant to orthogonal rotation after whitening, PCA alone conflates non-orthogonal biological sources and is easily hijacked by high-variance motion or physiological artifacts, whereas ICA exploits higher-order non-Gaussianity (Comon, 1994; Hyvärinen & Oja, 2000) to unmix independent sources up to permutation, sign, and scale. Knowing these identifiability boundaries prevents researchers from interpreting PCA axes as independent neural generators or applying ICA to purely Gaussian subspaces.

references.authors: Comon P
references.title: Independent component analysis, A new concept?
references.takeaway: Formalizes Independent Component Analysis and proves via the Darmois-Skitovich theorem that non-Gaussian independent sources are identifiable up to permutation, sign, and scale.

references.authors: Hyvärinen A, Oja E
references.title: Independent component analysis: algorithms and applications
references.takeaway: Derives the fixed-point FastICA algorithm maximizing non-Gaussianity (negentropy/kurtosis) on pre-whitened data.

references.authors: Beckmann C, Smith S
references.title: Probabilistic Independent Component Analysis for Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging
references.takeaway: Introduces Probabilistic ICA (FSL MELODIC), using PCA rank estimation in a Gaussian noise subspace prior to spatial ICA decomposition of fMRI data.

references.authors: Du Y, Fu Z, Sui J, Gao S, Xing Y, Lin D, Salman M, Abrol A, Rahaman MA, Chen J, Hong LE, Kochunov P, Osuch EA, Calhoun VD
references.title: NeuroMark: An automated and adaptive ICA based pipeline to identify reproducible fMRI markers of brain disorders
references.takeaway: Introduces NeuroMark, a spatially constrained ICA framework that extracts reproducible subject-specific functional network biomarkers across multi-site fMRI cohorts.

lessons.technique: Unsupervised clustering, Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), silhouette validation, and bootstrap stability analysis
lessons.why_it_matters: Clustering algorithms drive both cortical parcellation (Yeo et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2013; Schaefer et al., 2018) and clinical 'biotype' discovery in psychiatric neuroimaging. Because k-means and spectral algorithms partition any continuous distribution—even an isotropic or elongated Gaussian cloud—into compact regions with highly significant post-hoc ANOVA p-values (Dinga et al., 2019), unvalidated cluster claims frequently reflect unstandardized nuisance variance, circular double-dipping, or low test-retest reliability (Elliott et al., 2020). Combining permutation-invariant metrics (ARI; Hubert & Arabie, 1985) with resampling stability curves (Lange et al., 2004) and longitudinal noise audits is mandatory before claiming discrete neurobiological subtypes.

references.authors: Hubert L, Arabie P
references.title: Comparing partitions
references.takeaway: Derives the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), correcting pairwise partition agreement for chance under a hypergeometric permutation null.

references.authors: Rousseeuw PJ
references.title: Silhouettes: A graphical aid to the interpretation and validation of cluster analysis
references.venue: Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics
references.takeaway: Introduces the silhouette coefficient to quantify within-cluster cohesion relative to nearest-neighbor cluster separation.

references.authors: Lange T, Roth V, Braun ML, Buhmann JM
references.title: Stability-Based Validation of Clustering Solutions
references.takeaway: Formalizes stability-based cluster validation by measuring partition reproducibility across resampled splits and selecting K against null stability baselines.

references.authors: Dinga R, Schmaal L, Penninx BW, van Tol MJ, Veltman DJ, van Velzen L, Mennes M, van der Wee NJ, Marquand AF
references.title: Evaluating the evidence for biotypes of depression: Methodological replication and extension of
references.takeaway: Shows that apparent neuroimaging depression biotypes can arise from clustering continuous distributions without proper null-distribution and stability controls.

lessons.technique: Functional and structural connectomes, graph topology metrics (degree, density, clustering, modularity), and Connectome-Based Predictive Modeling (CPM)
lessons.why_it_matters: Graph-theoretic network analysis (Brain Connectivity Toolbox; Rubinov & Sporns, 2010) and Connectome-Based Predictive Modeling (CPM; Shen et al., 2017) are standard frameworks for relating inter-regional functional and diffusion connectivity to cognition and clinical phenotypes. Without rigorous confound regression, residual head motion creates systematic distance-dependent correlation artifacts (Power et al., 2012), arbitrary binarization thresholds either fuse communities or shatter graphs (van den Heuvel et al., 2017), and screening edges across the full sample before cross-validation fabricates high predictive correlations from pure noise. Learning threshold sensitivity curves and strictly nested in-fold edge screening protects connectome studies from artifactual topology and circularity.

references.authors: Bullmore E, Sporns O
references.title: Complex brain networks: graph theoretical analysis of structural and functional systems
references.takeaway: Establishes the graph-theoretic framework for analyzing segregation, integration, and hub topology in structural and functional brain networks.

references.authors: Rubinov M, Sporns O
references.title: Complex network measures of brain connectivity: Uses and interpretations
references.takeaway: Defines the standard mathematical formulations and Brain Connectivity Toolbox implementations for degree, clustering coefficient, path length, and modularity in brain graphs.

references.authors: van den Heuvel MP, de Lange SC, Zalesky A, Seguin C, Yeo BT, Schmidt R
references.title: Proportional thresholding in resting-state fMRI functional connectivity networks and consequences for patient-control connectome studies: Issues and recommendations
references.takeaway: Demonstrates how both absolute and proportional thresholding can confound graph topology metrics with overall functional connectivity strength and noise differences between groups.

references.authors: Dadi K, Rahim M, Abraham A, Chyzhyk D, Milham M, Thirion B, Varoquaux G
references.title: Benchmarking functional connectome-based predictive models for resting-state fMRI
references.takeaway: Benchmarks functional connectome predictive pipelines across large cohorts, showing how parcellation, tangent-space parameterization, and in-fold regularization govern generalization.

lessons.technique: Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA), Representational Dissimilarity Matrices (RDMs), cross-validated distances (crossnobis), and condition-label permutation inference
lessons.why_it_matters: Representational Similarity Analysis (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Nili et al., 2014; rsatoolbox) enables quantitative comparison between brain regions, species, and deep neural network layers by abstracting from voxel coordinates to second-order pairwise condition distances. However, uncrossvalidated squared Euclidean or Mahalanobis distances suffer a strictly positive quadratic noise bias that converts heteroscedastic trial noise (e.g., high-motion or low-trial conditions) into illusory representational clusters (Walther et al., 2016). Using cross-validated distance estimators across independent imaging runs and permuting condition labels jointly across rows and columns are essential for unbiased geometry inference (Schütt et al., 2023).

references.authors: Nili H, Wingfield C, Walther A, Su L, Marslen-Wilson W, Kriegeskorte N
references.title: A Toolbox for Representational Similarity Analysis
references.takeaway: Introduces the Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) toolbox, condition-label permutation testing, and Kendall's tau-a rank correlation for models with tied dissimilarities.

references.authors: Walther A, Nili H, Ejaz N, Alink A, Kriegeskorte N, Diedrichsen J
references.title: Reliability of dissimilarity measures for multi-voxel pattern analysis
references.takeaway: Proves that uncrossvalidated distance estimators suffer positive noise bias and demonstrates that cross-validated Mahalanobis (crossnobis) distances restore unbiased zero-centered geometry.

references.authors: Diedrichsen J, Kriegeskorte N
references.title: Representational models: A common framework for understanding encoding, pattern-component, and representational-similarity analysis
references.takeaway: Unifies encoding models, pattern component modeling, and second-order RSA matrices under a common second-moment representational geometry framework.

references.authors: Schütt HH, Kipnis AD, Diedrichsen J, Kriegeskorte N
references.title: Statistical inference on representational geometries
references.takeaway: Establishes rsatoolbox 3.0's cross-validated bootstrap and two-factor (subject-by-stimulus) statistical inference framework for comparing representational geometries.

lessons.technique: Multivariate searchlight mapping, radius bias-variance-dilation trade-offs, and whole-brain multiple-testing control
lessons.why_it_matters: Spherical and surface-based searchlight mapping (Kriegeskorte et al., 2006; Nilearn, BrainIAK, PyMVPA) is the standard technique for localizing multivariate pattern information across the brain when regions of interest are not fixed a priori. Because any sphere overlapping even a single informative voxel achieves above-chance decoding, searchlight maps dilate true spatial boundaries by the sphere radius r in every direction—a fundamental interpretation pitfall established by Etzel, Zacks & Braver (2013)—while scanning thousands of centers requires non-parametric permutation FWER control (Stelzer et al., 2013). Understanding radius dilation and multi-center false positives prevents researchers from mistaking smoothed sphere footprints for fine-grained cortical boundaries.

references.title: Information-based functional brain mapping
references.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
references.takeaway: Introduces spherical multivariate searchlight mapping to scan local multi-voxel pattern information across the brain without pre-specifying regions of interest.

references.authors: Stelzer J, Chen Y, Turner R
references.title: Statistical inference and multiple testing correction in classification-based multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA): Random permutations and cluster size control
references.takeaway: Develops non-parametric permutation and cluster-size family-wise error correction specifically tailored for whole-brain MVPA searchlight maps.

references.authors: Etzel JA, Zacks JM, Braver TS
references.title: Searchlight analysis: Promise, pitfalls, and potential
references.takeaway: Demonstrates the center-voxel attribution fallacy and spatial dilation artifacts in searchlight maps, showing how a single informative voxel inflates apparent cluster radius.

references.authors: Weaverdyck ME, Lieberman MD, Parkinson C
references.title: Tools of the Trade Multivoxel pattern analysis in fMRI: a practical introduction for social and affective neuroscientists
references.takeaway: Provides a modern methodological guide to MVPA and searchlight analysis, covering radius trade-offs, cross-validation hygiene, and spatial specificity limits.

lessons.technique: Inter-subject correlation (ISC), buffered naturalistic encoding models, and orthogonal Procrustes functional alignment
lessons.why_it_matters: Naturalistic movie and story paradigms drive continuous multi-network brain dynamics without artificial trial structure, requiring leave-one-out inter-subject correlation (BrainIAK / Nastase et al., 2019), buffered temporal encoding splits (Huth et al., 2016), and functional alignment across brains (Hyperalignment / SRM / MindEye2). Without leave-one-out exclusion, correlating a participant with the all-subject group mean injects self-noise that yields an expected correlation of 1/sqrt(S) even on pure white noise; without temporal buffer gaps, hemodynamic and stimulus autocorrelation leak across train/test boundaries; and without functional alignment, fine-scale topographic differences across participants attenuate shared multi-voxel signals.

references.authors: Hasson U, Nir Y, Levy I, Fuhrmann G, Malach R
references.title: Intersubject Synchronization of Cortical Activity During Natural Vision
references.takeaway: Introduces voxel-by-voxel inter-subject correlation during free viewing of natural movies to isolate shared stimulus-locked cortical responses.

references.authors: Nastase SA, Gazzola V, Hasson U, Keysers C
references.title: Measuring shared responses across subjects using intersubject correlation
references.takeaway: Formalizes the y = c + id + epsilon decomposition, leave-one-out vs. pairwise ISC estimators, and autocorrelation-preserving circular time-shift/phase-randomization/bootstrap inference.

references.authors: Haxby JV, Guntupalli JS, Connolly AC, Halchenko YO, Conroy BR, Gobbini MI, Hanke M, Ramadge PJ
references.title: A Common, High-Dimensional Model of the Representational Space in Human Ventral Temporal Cortex
references.takeaway: Establishes orthogonal Procrustes hyperalignment to map idiosyncratic individual voxel topographies into a shared functional representational space.

references.authors: Kumar M, Ellis CT, Lu Q, Zhang H, Capotă M, Willke TL, Ramadge PJ, Turk-Browne NB, Norman KA
references.title: BrainIAK tutorials: User-friendly learning materials for advanced fMRI analysis
references.takeaway: Provides the canonical open-source BrainIAK workflows for ISC, ISFC, circular time-shift permutation testing, and Shared Response Modeling.

lessons.technique: Linear Gaussian latent-variable generative modeling (Factor Analysis) and posterior predictive covariance checking
lessons.why_it_matters: Generative latent-variable models (Factor Analysis, PPCA, HMMs, VAEs) are used across neuroimaging to infer low-dimensional network drives, denoise multi-sensor recordings, and synthesize realistic brain data. Evaluating a generator only by whether it matches single-region means or 1D marginal histograms fails to detect complete loss of inter-regional functional connectivity (Cov(x_i, x_j) = 0), and using isotropic PCA instead of heteroscedastic Factor Analysis allows a single noisy sensor channel to hijack the leading latent components. Posterior predictive checks on held-out covariance matrices and higher-order statistics force explicit falsification of the assumed latent rank K and noise structure Psi.

references.authors: Rubin DB, Thayer DT
references.title: EM algorithms for ML factor analysis
references.takeaway: Derives the expectation-maximization algorithm for maximum-likelihood Factor Analysis with channel-specific diagonal uniquenesses Psi.

references.authors: Tipping ME, Bishop CM
references.title: Probabilistic Principal Component Analysis
references.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B
references.takeaway: Establishes the probabilistic latent-variable formulation of PCA (isotropic noise Psi = sigma^2 I) as a constrained special case of Factor Analysis.

references.authors: Rubin DB
references.title: Bayesianly Justifiable and Relevant Frequency Calculations for the Applied Statistician
references.takeaway: Introduces posterior predictive checking by comparing observed discrepancy statistics against synthetic replications drawn from the fitted model.

references.authors: Gabry J, Simpson D, Vehtari A, Betancourt M, Gelman A
references.title: Visualization in Bayesian workflow
references.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A
references.takeaway: Demonstrates modern graphical and quantitative posterior predictive checks for diagnosing generative model misspecification.

lessons.technique: Hidden Markov Models (HMMs): log-domain forward filtering, forward-backward smoothing, Viterbi decoding, and neural event segmentation
lessons.why_it_matters: Hidden Markov Models are widely used in resting-state fMRI (Vidaurre et al., 2017) and naturalistic movie/story paradigms (Baldassano et al., 2017; BrainIAK) to infer unlabelled state transitions, state-specific covariance networks, and narrative event boundaries. Without log-domain dynamic programming (logsumexp), multiplying observation likelihoods over hundreds of TRs underflows IEEE-754 floating-point arithmetic; without a temporal transition prior, instantaneous classifiers chatter across single-sample noise spikes; and without testing against stationary or continuous-drift baselines (Laumann et al., 2017), researchers can mistake discretized smooth fluctuations for biological state switches.

references.authors: Rabiner LR
references.title: A tutorial on hidden Markov models and selected applications in speech recognition
references.takeaway: Defines the canonical HMM formulation: forward-backward marginal smoothing, scaling/log-domain recursion to prevent underflow, Viterbi MAP decoding, and Baum-Welch EM.

references.authors: Baldassano C, Chen J, Zadbood A, Pillow JW, Hasson U, Norman KA
references.title: Discovering Event Structure in Continuous Narrative Perception and Memory
references.takeaway: Applies event-segmentation HMMs to naturalistic movie fMRI, revealing a cortical hierarchy of event timescales and hippocampal boundary responses.

references.authors: Laumann TO, Snyder AZ, Mitra A, Gordon EM, Gratton C, Adeyemo B, Gilmore AW, Nelson SM, Berg JJ, Greene DJ, McCarthy JE, Tagliazucchi E, Laufs H, Schlaggar BL, Dosenbach NUF, Petersen SE
references.title: On the Stability of BOLD fMRI Correlations
references.takeaway: Demonstrates that apparent resting-state fMRI state dynamics can arise from sampling variability, head motion, and arousal under a stationary process, motivating strict null testing.

lessons.technique: Linear Gaussian state-space filtering (Kalman filter) and Dynamic Causal Modeling (DCM) with regional hemodynamic forward models
lessons.why_it_matters: State-space models and Dynamic Causal Modeling (DCM in SPM; Friston et al., 2003; Zeidman et al., 2019) separate hidden neural state transitions from sluggish, noisy biophysical measurements. In Kalman filtering, misspecifying the observation noise variance R_assumed << R_true forces the filter to track observation noise while reporting deceptively small posterior uncertainty (a >900x calibration mismatch here); in fMRI connectivity, regional variations in hemodynamic time-to-peak (Handwerker et al., 2004) can reverse apparent BOLD temporal precedence and mislead lag-based Granger causality into inferring backwards directed connections (David et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2011).

references.authors: Kalman RE
references.title: A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems
references.takeaway: Derives the recursive Bayesian prediction-update filter and optimal Kalman gain for linear Gaussian dynamical systems.

references.authors: Friston KJ, Harrison L, Penny W
references.title: Dynamic causal modelling
references.takeaway: Formulates DCM for fMRI by coupling a bilinear directed neural state equation with a region-specific Balloon-Windkessel hemodynamic forward model.

references.authors: Smith SM, Miller KL, Salimi-Khorshidi G, Webster M, Beckmann CF, Nichols TE, Ramsey JD, Woolrich MW
references.title: Network modelling methods for FMRI
references.takeaway: Benchmarks directed and undirected connectivity methods on biophysical fMRI simulations, showing that lag-based Granger causality performs poorly under regional hemodynamic delay variability.

references.title: A guide to group effective connectivity analysis, part 1: First level analysis with DCM for fMRI
references.takeaway: Provides the modern practical specification, parameter prior, and model-validation workflow for first-level DCM in SPM.

lessons.technique: Convolutional neural network (CNN) weight sharing, analytical backpropagation, finite-difference gradient checking, and shortcut-learning audits
lessons.why_it_matters: Convolutional layers underpin 3D structural and functional MRI encoders (ResNets, U-Nets, BrainIAC, OpenMind) by sharing local kernel weights across space rather than fitting >10^8 dense parameters. However, hand-derived or custom backpropagation kernels can fail silently without centered finite-difference verification, and Empirical Risk Minimization will readily latch onto hospital-specific acquisition tags, field-of-view cropping, or corner calibration markers (shortcut learning; Zech et al., 2018; Geirhos et al., 2020), achieving near-100% internal accuracy while collapsing to chance on clean external scans.

references.title: Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition
references.takeaway: Introduces convolutional weight sharing and translation-equivariant feature maps optimized end-to-end by gradient descent.

references.takeaway: Introduces residual skip connections (ResNet), the backbone architecture used in BrainIAC (PM03) and OpenMind (PM04) 3D medical CNNs.

lessons.technique: Medical image segmentation evaluation (Dice vs. pixel accuracy under class imbalance), image-level splitting, and contrast-invariance
lessons.why_it_matters: Dense anatomical and lesion segmentation (U-Net, V-Net, nnU-Net, FastSurfer, SynthSeg) is pervasive in clinical neuroimaging, where focal lesions often occupy <1%–7% of voxels. Under severe foreground imbalance, pixel-wise accuracy exceeds 93%–99% for a trivial all-background dummy predictor that misses every lesion; splitting 2D slices instead of whole 3D participant volumes leaks nearly identical adjacent anatomy between train and test sets (Yagis et al., 2021); and models trained on raw single-sequence intensities fail under T1-to-T2/FLAIR contrast inversion unless trained with domain randomization (SynthSeg, Billot et al., 2023).

lessons.technique: Self-supervised pretraining (denoising autoencoders), frozen linear probing vs. end-to-end fine-tuning, and representation collapse auditing
lessons.why_it_matters: Self-supervised pretraining on large unlabeled MRI cohorts (BrainIAC on ~49k scans, OpenMind on ~114k volumes, MindEye2 across NSD subjects) learns low-dimensional representations that transfer to small clinical cohorts where labeled patients are scarce. When adapting a pretrained checkpoint, researchers must choose between freezing the encoder for a low-variance linear probe versus end-to-end fine-tuning (which can distort pretrained features on tiny labeled samples; Kumar et al., 2022), keep test cohorts strictly disjoint from unlabeled pretraining, and verify that the encoder has not suffered representation collapse (Chen & He, 2021).

lessons.technique: Scaled dot-product self-attention, permutation equivariance vs. positional encoding, variance-guided patch tokenization, and foundation model cards
lessons.why_it_matters: Transformer foundation models for 3D structural and 4D functional MRI (BrainSegFounder, Omni-fMRI) replace fixed local convolutions with all-to-all content-addressed self-attention. Without explicit 3D/4D positional encodings, self-attention is strictly permutation-equivariant and blind to brain anatomy; without motion quality control or despiking, high-amplitude head-motion spikes can hijack softmax attention weights or variance-sensitive patch tokenizers; and without a structured Model Card (Mitchell et al., 2019), studies risk violating biobank Material Transfer Agreements (e.g., UK Biobank MTA) or overclaiming universal superiority across tasks where specialized baselines (such as SwiFT on SALD age prediction) perform better.

lessons.technique: Probability calibration (Brier score, ECE, Platt/temperature scaling), permutation feature importance under collinearity, and cryptographic provenance ledgers
lessons.why_it_matters: Clinical and translational neuroimaging models are frequently judged by rank-based discrimination (ROC-AUC), yet a model with good ROC-AUC can produce severely overconfident risk probabilities that mislead clinical decision thresholds (Van Calster et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2017). Simultaneously, post-hoc explanations such as permutation importance or saliency maps can fail silently when brain regions are collinear (splitting importance under Ridge or arbitrarily zeroing one twin under Lasso; Strobl et al., 2008; Hooker et al., 2021) or when saliency maps act as weight-insensitive edge detectors (Adebayo et al., 2018). Post-hoc calibration on a disjoint split, grouped/conditional importance checks, and SHA-256 provenance ledgers are essential before claiming deployment readiness.

lessons.technique: End-to-end audit of anatomical spatial transformations (voxel-to-world affine geometry, grid resampling vs. registration, physical-space Gaussian smoothing, and categorical mask interpolation)
lessons.why_it_matters: Every structural and functional neuroimaging pipeline (such as fMRIPrep, FastSurfer, and SynthSeg) chains voxel-to-world affine transforms, grid resamplings, Gaussian smoothing, and mask interpolation before statistical modeling. Auditing these operations prevents conflating grid resampling with anatomical registration and stops continuous linear interpolation from corrupting binary or multi-class tissue masks with fractional perimeter erosion (~6.9% volume loss under integer truncation) or phantom boundary labels. It forces explicit choices of target grid geometry, physical smoothing kernel width in millimeters, and interpolation order matched to continuous versus categorical image semantics.

lessons.technique: First-level mass-univariate task-fMRI General Linear Model (BIDS time-axis alignment, HRF convolution, DCT drift filtering, AR(1) prewhitening, and voxelwise FDR inference)
lessons.why_it_matters: First-level GLM fitting translates a 4D functional MRI time series and stimulus event log into subject-level effect-size and statistical maps that feed every downstream group analysis or decoding study. Without verifying BIDS sidecar timing metadata, cosine drift cutoff frequencies, and residual autocorrelation, an analyst can silently desynchronize stimulus onsets from brain volumes, absorb the task regressor into high-pass drift columns (inflating variance by ~7x when the cutoff encroaches on the task frequency), or misstate single-session statistical precision. Auditing the GLM forces explicit decisions about dummy-scan provenance, high-pass cutoff relative to task period, prewhitening noise models, and reporting unthresholded effect and uncertainty maps alongside FDR-thresholded displays.

lessons.technique: Multi-site cohort prediction, participant-grouped cross-validation, location-scale scanner harmonization, and cluster-bootstrap uncertainty estimation
lessons.why_it_matters: Predictive neuroimaging models trained on multi-site cohorts routinely fail at new hospitals when they exploit scanner batch offsets or memorizable participant anatomy instead of invariant biological signal. Enforcing participant-grouped cross-validation, label-free location-scale harmonization, and person-level cluster bootstrapping prevents visit-level pseudoreplication (which narrows confidence intervals by ~17% in this benchmark) and exposes site-shortcut collapse (where inner-CV MAE = 0.400 degrades to held-out R² = -31.3). It forces researchers to separate development sites from held-out test sites, match the bootstrap resampling unit to the independent participant, and distinguish transductive feature harmonization from confirmatory out-of-site generalization.

lessons.technique: Supervised research plan verification, pseudoreplication auditing, multiverse specification-curve analysis, low-label transfer benchmarking, and Type M power analysis
lessons.why_it_matters: A runnable script or high benchmark score does not establish scientific validity if voxels are pseudoreplicated as independent participants, results depend on a cherry-picked preprocessing pipeline, or fine-tuned models latch onto local confounds. Auditing the full research plan—across observation units, a 16-pipeline specification curve, low-label transfer learning baselines, and sample-size power/Type M inflation—prevents false-positive explosions (82.8% null FPR under voxel pooling) and small-sample effect exaggeration (~5.3x at N=25 for r=0.08). It forces researchers to freeze confirmation boundaries before unblinding test cohorts and justify every transformation and uncertainty unit in an unscripted oral defense.
